<p class="lead">
  Training is one and the same cycle of five actions, repeated 1260 times. We will run
  it end to end on real data: from a handwritten digit turned into 64 numbers and random weights
  to 97.78% on images the network has never seen.
</p>

<p>
  The article is self-contained: every formula is derived right here, from the definition of the derivative and the chain
  rule, and none is taken ready-made “from a textbook”. The only math you need is the derivative
  of a composite function and matrix multiplication. Everything else is arithmetic you can check
  on a calculator: every key number in the article is computed and shown in full, together
  with the terms it was added up from.
</p>

<p>
  The dataset is <strong>digits</strong> from scikit-learn: 1797 handwritten digits at 8 × 8 resolution.
  It is a close relative of MNIST, only smaller: each cell here is the number of inked points
  in a 4 × 4 block of the original 32 × 32 scan, so the values are integers from 0 to 16.
  The small size is deliberate: the whole image fits on screen, all 64 numbers can be
  written out, and a full training run takes a fraction of a second, so any experiment in the article
  can be repeated and checked.
</p>

<div class="semantic-key" aria-label="Color key of the article">
  <span><i style="background:#3576C0"></i>data: images and labels</span>
  <span><i style="background:#C29E08"></i>parameters and operations</span>
  <span><i style="background:#73B222"></i>what the network computed</span>
  <span><i style="background:#C30B0A"></i>loss and gradients</span>
</div>

<p>
  One more rule works inside the diagrams: <strong>yellow is what gets trained</strong>
  (weights and biases), <strong>green is what is recomputed from scratch</strong> on every batch
  and then thrown away. The split into these two groups is the most useful thing to take from the first four parts.
</p>


<div class="callout-blue">
  <strong>How to use the interactives:</strong> press “Next” and look not at the whole diagram at once
  but only at the bright part. The blocks stay in place from step to step, so what switches
  is the meaning, not the picture in front of you. The forward and backward passes are shown twice: first shapes and
  formulas, then the same steps with the numbers plugged in. The ← → arrow keys work when a scene has focus.
  Besides the scenes, the article has six live widgets in frames: you can drag and click in them,
  and the numbers are computed right in the browser on the same images and weights.
</div>

## Part 1. What goes in

<p>
  A network does not work with images. It works with matrices of numbers, and the first thing to do is
  to turn one into the other faithfully. An 8 × 8 image is a grid of 64 cells, each holding an integer
  from 0 to 16. We divide them by 16 to get the range from 0 to 1 and lay the rows
  out one after another in a single row of length 64.
</p>

<p>
  This row is the <strong>feature vector</strong> of one image. The order of the cells in it is arbitrary
  but fixed: all that matters is that the same cell always lands in the same position.
  The fact that cells 11 and 12 were neighbors is lost for good:
  a fully connected network knows nothing about the geometry of the image and will not reconstruct it.
</p>

<p>A network that does use this neighborhood is called convolutional. How it works and what it gives on the same handwritten digits is covered in the article <a href="article.html?slug=cnn-from-zero">“A convolutional neural network from scratch”</a>.</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="X \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times 64}, \qquad Y \in \{0,1\}^{B \times 10}, \qquad \sum_{c} y_{ic} = 1"></div>

<p>
  The correct answer also becomes numbers: the class “3” is written as a row of ten numbers with
  a one in the fourth place, since the places stand for the digits 0 to 9. This encoding is called <strong>one-hot</strong>, and it is needed
  so that the network's answer and the truth can be compared with a single formula, without branching on the class number.
</p>

<div class="callout-blue">
  <strong>Why divide by 16:</strong> the maximum cell value in this dataset is 16,
  because a cell is the count of inked points in a 4 × 4 block. Dividing by the maximum is
  the simplest normalization. Without it, the same learning rate breaks the network:
  accuracy drops to 10%.
</div>

<p>Let's see step by step how one image becomes a row of the matrix.</p>

    <button type="button" data-nav="prev">← Back</button>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img" data-focus="img">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what an image is</div>
      <h4>A handwritten digit is an 8 × 8 grid</h4>
<p>The digits dataset from scikit-learn: 1797 handwritten digits, each shrunk to eight by eight cells. A cell holds an integer from 0 to 16, how much of that cell is inked. There are no “pixels” beyond that in this task: the image is fully described by 64 numbers.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img one" data-focus="one">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · a cell</div>
      <h4>One cell is one number, and half of them are zeros</h4>
<p>Across the whole training set, 48.93% of cells are zero: the digit sits in the middle and the margins are empty. Four cells, #1, #25, #33 and #40, are zero in all 1347 images at once.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="strip" data-focus="strip">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · a vector</div>
      <h4>The network does not know the image is square</h4>
<p>We divide the values by 16 (now they are from 0 to 1) and lay the rows out one after another in a single row of 64 numbers. The order is arbitrary but fixed once and for all: cell #11 must always land in position 11, otherwise the weights would learn on different places. The two-dimensional shape of the image is lost: a fully connected network knows nothing about which cells are neighbors.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="batch" data-focus="batch">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · a batch</div>
      <h4>Several images stack into a matrix</h4>
<p>The network computes not one image at a time but in batches. Four rows stacked on top of each other give a matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span> of shape 4 × 64: a row is an example, a column is a cell. From here on, all the arithmetic of the article is operations on such rectangles. In the real run a batch has 32 rows; no formula changes with the number of rows.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="onehot" data-focus="onehot">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · the correct answer</div>
      <h4>The label also becomes a row of numbers</h4>
<p>The class “3” is written as a row of ten numbers: the places stand for the digits 0 to 9, so the one is in the fourth place and the rest are zeros. This encoding is called one-hot. It is needed so that the network's answer (ten numbers) and the correct answer (ten numbers) can be compared with a single formula.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="split" data-focus="split">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · an honest test</div>
      <h4>450 images the network will never see</h4>
<p>The split is done once: 1347 images for training, 450 for the held-out set, with class proportions preserved. Everything we later call “accuracy” is measured on these 450. Otherwise an answer learned by heart could not be told apart from understanding.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>The scene showed one image. Below you can take any of the four digits in the batch or a random training one and check where each cell goes.</p>

<div class="hn-live" id="wiCells"></div>

<p>
  The split is done once and preserves class proportions: 1347 images in training, 450 in the held-out
  set, and in each part all ten digits are represented roughly equally. Everything called
  accuracy from here on is measured only on these 450.
</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> to the network, the data is exactly two matrices, X and Y, with the same
  number of rows. A row of X is an image, a row of Y is the correct answer. Everything else in the article will be
  arithmetic on these two rectangles.
</div>

  The weights are still random: this is how the network looks before the first training step.

    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img" data-focus="img"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · data</div><h4>The first image of the batch: a three</h4><p>This is the same image as in part 1: eight by eight cells, each holding a number from 0 to 16. It will run through the whole article: on it we will compute the forward pass, the loss and the backward pass.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat" data-focus="flat"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · input</div><h4>The image becomes a column of 64 numbers</h4><p>The cells are laid out row by row and divided by 16, giving <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x"></span> of 64 numbers from 0 to 1. In the diagram these are 64 squares from top to bottom: the bluer the square, the brighter the cell. The three has 34 inked cells; the other 30 are zero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat e1 h1 p1" data-focus="e1 h1 p1"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · first layer</div><h4>Each of the 32 neurons is connected to all 64 inputs</h4><p>Each connection has its own weight: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="64 \cdot 32 = 2048"></span> weights. A neuron multiplies each input by the weight of its connection, adds up the 64 products and adds its bias <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b_j"></span>. There are 32 biases, 2080 numbers in the layer in total.</p><p>The gray mesh is all 2048 connections. Highlighted in color are the three largest “input × weight” terms of each neuron: yellow ones pull the sum up, gray ones down, and the thickness shows the size. For empty cells the term is zero whatever the weight.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat e1 h1 relu p1" data-focus="relu"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · ReLU</div><h4>20 neurons out of 32 output zero</h4><p>After the sum, each neuron passes it through ReLU: a negative number becomes zero, a positive one passes as is. On the three the sum is positive for 12 neurons; their fill shows the value. The largest is neuron 22: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22} = 1.0536"></span>. The other 20 are drawn dashed: they output zero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat e1 h1 relu p1 e2 out p2" data-focus="e2 out p2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · second layer</div><h4>Ten scores, one per digit</h4><p>The second layer works the same way: each of the 10 outputs is connected to all 32 neurons, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="32 \cdot 10 = 320"></span> weights, 10 biases, 330 numbers in total. Again the color marks the largest “neuron value × weight” terms. The dashed neurons have no colored lines: zero times any weight is zero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat e1 h1 relu p1 e2 out p2 soft" data-focus="soft"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · softmax</div><h4>Scores turn into probabilities</h4><p>Softmax turns ten scores into ten positive numbers that sum to 1. All of them are close to 10%: the weights are still random and the network has learned nothing. The three got the most, 14.88%, but that is a coincidence: on all held-out images the same network is right 12.44% of the time.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat e1 h1 relu p1 e2 out p2 soft tot" data-focus="tot"><div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · total</div><h4>2410 numbers for the whole network</h4><p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="2080 + 330 = 2410"></span>. The first layer holds 86.3% of the parameters: it is the only one that looks at all 64 cells at once. Right now these numbers are chosen at random. Training the network means choosing them so that for the three output 3 wins by a wide margin, and likewise for every image.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the network's input is 64 independent numbers, and everything the network can do lives
  in the connection weights and neuron biases: 2080 numbers in the first layer and 330 in the second.
</div>

---

## Part 3. One layer is one matrix

<p>
  The graph has 2048 + 320 = 2368 connections, and computing on it connection by connection is awkward. The weights of one layer
  are put into a table: a row is responsible for an input, a column for a neuron. This table is the
  <strong>weight matrix</strong> <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span> of shape 64 × 32, and the whole layer is computed with one multiplication:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="\mathbf h^{(1)} = \max\left(0,\ \mathbf x W^{(1)} + \mathbf b^{(1)}\right), \qquad [1\times 64]\cdot[64\times 32] = [1\times 32]"></div>

<div class="callout-blue">
  <strong>About the indices:</strong> in <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(1)}_{kj}"></span> the superscript is the layer number, and the subscripts read
  “from → to”: from input <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_k"></span> into neuron <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j"></span>. So <span class="math-inline" data-tex="k"></span> is the row number of
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span>, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="j"></span> is the column number.
</div>

<p>Let's see step by step how the connections of the graph turn into cells of the matrix.</p>

    <button type="button" data-nav="prev">← Back</button>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid" data-focus="edges nodes"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · structure</div><h4>Every input is connected to every neuron</h4><p>This is the first layer from part 2, only enlarged and not in full: five of the 64 inputs and four of the 32 neurons are drawn. There are 64 · 32 = 2048 connections, one for each “input, neuron” pair. On the right is the table where we are about to put their weights.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid one" data-focus="one"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · one connection</div><h4>One connection, one weight, one cell</h4><p>The connection from <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_2"></span> to <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22}"></span> carries the weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(1)}_{2,22} = 0.1160"></span>. The superscript is the layer number, the subscripts read “from, to”. Put the weight in row 2, column 22: the input number becomes the row number and the neuron number becomes the column number. This way each of the 2048 connections gets its own cell, and we get a 64 × 32 table.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid row" data-focus="row"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · a row</div><h4>Everything leaving one input is a row of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span></h4><p>32 connections leave cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_2"></span>, one into each neuron. Their weights sit in the second row of the matrix. A row tells how one cell of the image affects all neurons of the layer at once.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid col" data-focus="col"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · a column</div><h4>Everything entering one neuron is a column of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span></h4><p>64 connections enter neuron <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22}"></span>, one from each cell. Their weights sit in column 22. To compute a neuron you need exactly the column: these are its 64 weights, one per image cell.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid col dot" data-focus="dot"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · one neuron</div><h4>A neuron is the input times its column</h4><p>A neuron multiplies each input by the weight of its connection and adds them up: this is the dot product of the row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x"></span> and column 22. On our three:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} z_{22} = 0\cdot 0.2416 + 0.0625\cdot 0.1160 + 0.5\cdot 0.1114 + 0.875\cdot 0.1284 + \ldots \\ = 1.0536 \end{gathered}"></div><p>There are 34 nonzero terms, one per inked cell. This is the same neuron 22 with the brightest fill in part 2.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid mat l1one in1" data-focus="mat l1one in1"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · the whole layer</div><h4>All 32 neurons are one multiplication <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x W^{(1)}"></span></h4><p>Each neuron is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x"></span> times its column. Doing this for all 32 columns at once gives a row times a matrix: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="[1\times 64]\cdot[64\times 32] = [1\times 32]"></span>. The inner sizes must match, and they are circled: the 64 numbers of the input meet the 64 rows of the matrix. What remains outside is a row of 32 numbers, one per neuron.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes grid bias mat l1one" data-focus="bias l1one"><div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · bias and ReLU</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf h^{(1)} = \max(0,\ \mathbf x W^{(1)} + \mathbf b^{(1)})"></span></h4><p>Each neuron has one more number, the bias <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b_j"></span>. All 32 biases form a row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf b^{(1)}"></span> of shape 1 × 32 and are added cell by cell. At the start of training the biases are zero. Then ReLU zeroes the negative cells, and the shape stays 1 × 32. The layer has <span class="math-inline" data-tex="64\cdot 32 + 32 = 2080"></span> parameters.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes g2 grid2 one2 mat l1one l2one in2" data-focus="g2 grid2 one2 l2one in2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 8 · second layer</div><h4>The second layer is one more matrix, 32 × 10</h4><p>Add the output layer to the graph: ten nodes, one per digit. Each is connected to all 32 neurons, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="32\cdot 10 = 320"></span> connections. Their weights go into a table by the same rule: the row is where the connection comes from, that is, a hidden neuron, and the column is where it goes, that is, a digit. This gives <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(2)}"></span> of shape 32 × 10.</p><p>Highlighted is the connection from neuron 22 to the output of digit “3”: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(2)}_{22,4} = 0.2681"></span>. Columns are numbered from one and digits from zero, so the three is in column 4.</p><p>The row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf h^{(1)}"></span> becomes the input of the second layer, and the multiplication repeats: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="[1\times 32]\cdot[32\times 10] + [1\times 10] = [1\times 10]"></span>. The whole network is two matrices and two rows of biases.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="edges nodes g2 grid2 mat l1B l2B" data-focus="l1B l2B"><div class="step-kicker">Step 9 · a batch</div><h4>Four images, four rows</h4><p>Take four images at once and stack their rows: this gives <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span> of shape 4 × 64. The product <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X W^{(1)}"></span> computes each row separately with the same matrix, so row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> of the result is the neurons of image <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span>. The formulas do not change; only the first number in the shape does: 1 became 4.</p><p>That is why from here on the network is drawn as matrices, not as a graph: 2368 connections cannot be told apart in a diagram, while the shapes are visible at once.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>
  In step 5, neuron 22 added 64 products into one number, 1.0536. Let's look at all 64 at once.
  Column 22 has as many numbers as the image has cells, so it can be folded into an 8 × 8 square
  and put next to the three: each weight lands in the cell it multiplies.
</p>

    <div class="step-panel" data-on="gx" data-focus="gx"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · data</div><h4>The three that neuron 22 computes on</h4><p>This is the first image of the batch from part 1. Each cell holds a number from 0 to 16; the network receives it divided by 16. 34 of the 64 cells are inked; the other 30 are zero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="gx k2 opa gw" data-focus="gw k2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · parameter</div><h4>Column 22 can be folded into a square too</h4><p>64 weights enter neuron 22, one per cell. This is column 22 of the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span> from the scene above. Put the weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w_{k,22}"></span> in the same cell where the image has <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_k"></span>. Cell 2 is circled: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_2 = 1/16 = 0.0625"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w_{2,22} = 0.1160"></span>, the very connection from step 2 of the scene above.</p><p>The weights are still random, so they do not look like a picture: yellow ones are positive, gray ones negative.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="gx opa gw opb gp hi" data-focus="gp hi"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · operation</div><h4>Cell by cell: 64 multiplications</h4><p>The neuron multiplies each cell of the image by the weight in the same cell. The largest contribution comes from the cell in row 8, column 4:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="x_{60}\,w_{60,22} = \tfrac{12}{16}\cdot 0.3459 = 0.2594"></div><p>Green cells push the sum up, gray ones down.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="gx opa gw opb gp zero" data-focus="zero"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · operation</div><h4>Under an empty cell the weight does nothing</h4><p>The weight of the column with the largest absolute value, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="0.4214"></span>, sits in row 3, column 8. On the three this cell is empty, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_{24} = 0"></span>, and the product is zero. The same holds for all 30 empty cells: their weights have no effect on this image, however large they are.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="gx opa gw opb gp sum" data-focus="sum"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · result</div><h4>Adding up 34 contributions</h4><div class="math-display" data-tex="z_{22} = \sum_{k=1}^{64} x_k\,w_{k,22} + b_{22}"></div><p>22 cells give <span class="math-inline" data-tex="+1.7517"></span> together, 12 cells give <span class="math-inline" data-tex="−0.6982"></span>. The bias before training is zero. The sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="1.0536"></span> is positive, and ReLU passes it as is: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22} = 1.0536"></span>, the same number as in step 5 of the scene above.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="gx gw gp sum row k2row" data-focus="row k2row"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · notation</div><h4>The same 64 products in a row</h4><p>Unfold both squares back into rows: the image becomes the row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x"></span>, and the weights become column 22 laid on its side. Cell 2 is circled here too. Under each pair stands its product; empty cells have no bar.</p><p>The sum of the 64 bars is exactly the dot product of a row and a column, which computes one neuron in <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x W^{(1)}"></span>.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>How such layers nest inside each other when there are more than two is covered in the article <a href="article.html?slug=nn-matryoshka">“A neural network as a nesting doll: building it layer by layer”</a>.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the connection from input <span class="math-inline" data-tex="k"></span> to neuron <span class="math-inline" data-tex="j"></span> is cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(k, j)"></span>
  of the weight matrix. A row is everything leaving one input, a column is everything entering one neuron,
  and the whole layer is the input row times the matrix plus the row of biases.
</div>

---

## Part 4. The network: 2410 numbers between the image and the answer

<p>
  The architecture is as ordinary as it gets: 64 inputs, one hidden layer of 32 neurons, 10 outputs.
  Between them is <strong>ReLU</strong>, at the output <strong>softmax</strong>. ReLU is essential here: without it the two linear layers would collapse into one, because the product of two matrices is again a matrix. No convolutions, normalization
  or residual connections: everything needed for a full training cycle is already here, and extra details
  would only get in the way of seeing the cycle as a whole.
</p>

<table class="shape-table">
  <tr><th>Object</th><th>What it is</th><th>Shape</th><th>Numbers</th></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span></td><td>batch of images</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="B"></span> × 64</td><td>recomputed</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(1)}"></span></td><td>first linear layer</td><td>64 × 32 and 32</td><td>2080</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(1)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H^{(1)}"></span></td><td>before and after ReLU</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="B"></span> × 32</td><td>recomputed</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(2)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(2)}"></span></td><td>second linear layer</td><td>32 × 10 and 10</td><td>330</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(2)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="P"></span></td><td>scores and probabilities</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="B"></span> × 10</td><td>recomputed</td></tr>
  <tr><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="L"></span></td><td>batch loss</td><td>number</td><td>—</td></tr>
</table>

<p>
  In total, <strong>2410 trainable numbers</strong>, and 86.3% of them live in the first layer: it is the only one
  that looks at all 64 cells at once. The size of the hidden layer is the only freedom we
  used; here is what it gives with everything else equal:
</p>

<table class="shape-table">
  <tr><th>Hidden layer</th><th>4</th><th>8</th><th>16</th><th>32</th><th>64</th><th>128</th></tr>
  <tr><td>parameters</td><td>310</td><td>610</td><td>1210</td><td>2410</td><td>4810</td><td>9610</td></tr>
  <tr><td>accuracy, %</td><td>79.56</td><td>92.44</td><td>96.67</td><td>97.78</td><td>98.00</td><td>98.00</td></tr>
</table>

<p>
  Thirty-two neurons is the point after which growth almost stops: doubling and quadrupling
  the network add only 0.22 percentage points. So from here on the article uses 64 → 32 → 10 everywhere.
</p>

<p>Let's see step by step what the network consists of and what in it is trained.</p>

      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · the whole network</div>
      <h4>The whole network converges to one number</h4>
<p>The last card takes two inputs at once: the answer P and the labels Y. The output is one number for the whole batch. This is the number that will decrease during training, and it is the one whose derivatives are taken with respect to all 2410 parameters.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="inp lin1 par1 relu lin2 par2 soft out loss count" data-focus="count">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · what is trained here</div>
      <h4>Only what hangs under the cards is trained</h4>
<p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(1)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(2)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(2)}"></span> are the state of the network: 2410 numbers that change step by step and live between batches. <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H^{(1)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(2)}"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="P"></span> are recomputed from scratch for each batch and thrown away. To train the network means to choose the 2410 numbers so that the second group gives the right answer.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the network is 2410 numbers plus a rule for applying them.
  The numbers live between batches and change during training; everything else, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="P"></span>, is born anew on every
  batch and thrown away right after. To train the network means to choose the first group so that the second
  gives the right answer.
</div>

---

## Part 5. The anatomy of training: how all models work

<p>
  The model is assembled: a rule and 2410 random numbers in it. Before computing anything, let's look at training
  as a whole. Its skeleton is the same for any model trained by gradient descent: the contents of the
  blocks change, but not their order.
</p>

<p>Let's see step by step which blocks training consists of.</p>

<div class="stage" id="stageCY" tabindex="0" aria-label="The anatomy of training">
  <div class="stage-figure">
<svg class="mg" id="cy" viewBox="0 0 960 522" role="img" aria-label="The anatomy of training: Task, Data, Model, Loss and the loop between them on the example of the 64, 32, 10 network">
<defs><marker id="cy-arw" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#5E5850"/></marker><marker id="cy-arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#C30B0A"/></marker><marker id="cy-arb" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#3576C0"/></marker></defs>
<defs><marker id="cy-ary" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#8F7406"/></marker></defs>
<text x="480" y="34" font-size="13" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">Task · Data · Model · Loss: one and the same frame for all models</text>
<rect x="30" y="54" width="376" height="432" rx="14" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#D8D4C8" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="54" y="92" font-size="20" fill="#111111" text-anchor="start" font-weight="800">The anatomy of training</text>
<text x="54" y="124" font-size="15" fill="#111111" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">For any model, from linear regression</text>
<text x="54" y="146" font-size="15" fill="#111111" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">to GPT, training works the same way.</text>
<text x="54" y="186" font-size="15" fill="#111111" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Four blocks</text>
<text x="54" y="214" font-size="15" fill="#3576C0" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Task</text>
<foreignObject x="122" y="191" width="270" height="36"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:15px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span>what we are doing at all</span></div></foreignObject>
<text x="54" y="242" font-size="15" fill="#3576C0" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Data</text>
<foreignObject x="122" y="219" width="270" height="36"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:15px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span>examples <span data-tex="(\mathbf x,\ \mathbf y)"></span></span></div></foreignObject>
<text x="54" y="270" font-size="15" fill="#3576C0" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Model</text>
<foreignObject x="122" y="247" width="270" height="36"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:15px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span>what we train</span></div></foreignObject>
<text x="54" y="298" font-size="15" fill="#C30B0A" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">Loss</text>
<foreignObject x="122" y="275" width="270" height="36"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:15px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span>how wrong it is</span></div></foreignObject>
<text x="54" y="346" font-size="15" fill="#111111" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">One loop, 1260 repetitions</text>

<text x="192" y="381" font-size="15" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">the model predicts</text>
<foreignObject x="54" y="393" width="130" height="30"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:15px;color:#111111;font-weight:400" data-tex="L(\mathbf p,\ \mathbf y)"></div></foreignObject>

<text x="192" y="445" font-size="15" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">the model is updated</text>
<g data-key="task"><rect x="620" y="54" width="240" height="62" rx="14" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#3576C0" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="740" y="80" font-size="17" fill="#3576C0" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Task</text><text x="740" y="102" font-size="13" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">recognize a digit: 10 classes</text><line x1="740" y1="118" x2="740" y2="146" stroke="#5E5850" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#cy-arw)"/></g>
<g data-key="loss"><rect x="620" y="150" width="240" height="92" rx="14" fill="#FFF7F7" stroke="#C30B0A" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="740" y="176" font-size="17" fill="#C30B0A" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Loss</text><foreignObject x="630" y="186" width="220" height="26"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:16px;color:#111111;font-weight:400" data-tex="L = -\log p_{y}"></div></foreignObject><text x="740" y="228" font-size="12.5" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">cross-entropy, one number</text></g>
<g data-key="data"><rect x="424" y="264" width="122" height="110" rx="14" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#3576C0" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="485" y="294" font-size="17" fill="#3576C0" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="700">Data</text><foreignObject x="430" y="306" width="110" height="26"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:16px;color:#111111;font-weight:400" data-tex="(\mathbf x,\ \mathbf y)"></div></foreignObject><text x="485" y="348" font-size="12.5" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">1347 images</text><line x1="548" y1="290" x2="616" y2="212" stroke="#5E5850" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#cy-arw)"/><line x1="548" y1="348" x2="616" y2="426" stroke="#5E5850" stroke-width="1.6" marker-end="url(#cy-arw)"/><foreignObject x="551" y="224" width="30" height="24"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:15px;color:#3576C0;font-weight:400" data-tex="\mathbf y"></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="551" y="390" width="30" height="24"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:15px;color:#3576C0;font-weight:400" data-tex="\mathbf x"></div></foreignObject></g>

<g data-key="cycle" data-only="1"><path d="M 680 394 C 628 358 628 280 680 244" fill="none" stroke="#8F7406" stroke-width="2.8" marker-end="url(#cy-ary)"/><path d="M 800 244 C 852 280 852 358 800 394" fill="none" stroke="#C30B0A" stroke-width="2.8" stroke-dasharray="7 5" marker-end="url(#cy-arr)"/><rect x="658" y="292" width="164" height="54" rx="27" fill="#FFFBEB" stroke="#C29E08" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="740" y="311" font-size="12" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="400">one training step</text><foreignObject x="660" y="317" width="160" height="26"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:14px;color:#111111;font-weight:400" data-tex="\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\nabla_\theta L"></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="576" y="293" width="50" height="26"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:16px;color:#8F7406;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\mathbf p"></span></span></div></foreignObject><text x="626" y="338" font-size="12.5" fill="#8F7406" text-anchor="end" font-weight="700">forward</text><foreignObject x="854" y="293" width="70" height="26"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit svg-math-center" style="font-size:16px;color:#9C0908;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\nabla_\theta L"></span></span></div></foreignObject><text x="854" y="338" font-size="12.5" fill="#9C0908" text-anchor="start" font-weight="700">backward</text></g>
<text x="40" y="508" font-size="13" fill="#5E5850" text-anchor="start" font-weight="400">blue blocks: what the task sets · red: what measures the miss and produces gradients</text>
</svg>
  </div>
  <div class="stage-bar">
    <button type="button" data-nav="prev">← Back</button>
    <button type="button" data-nav="next">Next →</button>
    <div class="stage-progress"></div>
    <div class="stage-counter"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="task loss data model" data-focus="task loss data model"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · four blocks</div><h4>A frame that does not change</h4><p>Every machine learning problem has a Task, Data, a Model and a Loss. Everything else is details: which model exactly sits inside and how the gradient is computed.</p><p>We already assembled the model in parts 2–4. From here the article goes around this frame: each following part computes one of its links by hand.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="task" data-focus="task"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · Task</div><h4>The task determines everything else</h4><p>We recognize a digit, that is, we pick one class out of ten. Hence the network's output: ten probabilities via softmax, and the loss: cross-entropy. If we predicted a number, say a price, the output would be one number and the squared error.</p><p>The Task is not chosen: it comes with the problem.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="data" data-focus="data"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · Data</div><h4>Pairs “input → correct answer”</h4><p>We have 1347 training images: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x"></span> is 64 numbers, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf y"></span> is a row of ten numbers with a single one. Another 450 images are held out and take no part in training: at the end we will use them to check that the network recognizes digits it has not seen.</p><p>The data does not change during training and limits what the model can learn.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="model" data-focus="model"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · Model</div><h4>What we train</h4><p>Here it is the 64 → 32 → 10 network: the rule <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf p = \mathrm{softmax}\big(\max(0,\ \mathbf x W^{(1)} + \mathbf b^{(1)})\, W^{(2)} + \mathbf b^{(2)}\big)"></span> and 2410 numbers <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\theta"></span> in it. The rule is fixed; the numbers change.</p><p>The model takes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf x"></span> and outputs <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf p"></span>. Nothing more is required of it.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="loss" data-focus="loss"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · Loss</div><h4>One number that can be decreased</h4><p>The Loss compares <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf p"></span> with the correct answer and outputs one number: minus the logarithm of the probability of the correct class, averaged over the batch. Forty probabilities of a batch cannot tell which network is better, but one number can.</p><p>This number has a derivative with respect to each of the 2410 parameters. That derivative is what the backward pass is for.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="task loss data model cycle" data-focus="cycle"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · the cycle</div><h4>Predictions forward, gradients backward</h4><p>The model passes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf p"></span> to the Loss, the Loss returns gradients to the Model, and the parameters move one step against the gradient. One turn is one training step. We have 42 steps per epoch and 30 epochs, 1260 turns in total.</p><p>Next we go around this circle part by part: the forward pass in parts 6 and 7, the loss in part 8, the backward pass in parts 9–11, the step in part 12, and the whole cycle with batches and epochs in part 13.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>One training step is five actions. For our network they look like this:</p>

<table class="shape-table">
  <tr><th>Action</th><th>What is computed</th><th>Part</th></tr>
  <tr><td>1. take a batch</td><td>32 images: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span> and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Y"></span></td><td>13</td></tr>
  <tr><td>2. forward pass</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="P = \mathrm{softmax}\big(\max(0,\ X W^{(1)} + b^{(1)})\, W^{(2)} + b^{(2)}\big)"></span></td><td>6, 7</td></tr>
  <tr><td>3. loss</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="L = -\tfrac{1}{B}\sum_i \log p_{i,\,y_i}"></span></td><td>8</td></tr>
  <tr><td>4. backward pass</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)},\ \partial L/\partial b^{(1)},\ \partial L/\partial W^{(2)},\ \partial L/\partial b^{(2)}"></span></td><td>9–11</td></tr>
  <tr><td>5. step</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \partial L/\partial \theta"></span></td><td>12</td></tr>
</table>

<p>
  After repeating these five actions 1260 times, the network recognizes 97.78% of the held-out images (part 13).
  We will take the links apart on one and the same batch of four images: a three, a five, a two and an eight.
</p>

<p>The same frame on a model with two numbers, where the whole cycle fits on one screen, is worked through in the article <a href="article.html?slug=linear-regression-full-cycle">“Linear regression: the full training cycle on three numbers”</a>.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> training is the cycle “batch → forward pass → loss → backward
  pass → step”. Task and Data set what to compute, the Model what to compute it with, the Loss what to decrease.
</div>

---

## Part 6. The forward pass: shapes first

<p>
  The first action of the cycle is the forward pass. On the graph in part 2 we followed one image; now
  we compute the whole batch of four images at once, with the matrices from part 3.
</p>

<p>
  The forward pass is four lines of arithmetic. Before plugging numbers into them, it is worth making sure
  the shapes match: almost all bugs in network code are mixed-up dimensions, and they are caught
  on paper in a minute.
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="Z^{(1)} = X W^{(1)} + b^{(1)}, \qquad H^{(1)} = \max\left(0, Z^{(1)}\right)"></div>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="Z^{(2)} = H^{(1)} W^{(2)} + b^{(2)}, \qquad P = \mathrm{softmax}\left(Z^{(2)}\right)"></div>

<p>
  We keep examples in rows: a row of the matrix is one image, and multiplication goes as
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X W"></span>, not <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W x"></span>. This convention differs from what is convenient when
  working through a single example (there a vector is usually written as a column), but it is the one used in all
  libraries, because it handles a batch without a single extra index.
</p>

<div class="callout-blue">
  <strong>What “contracting dimensions” means:</strong> in the product [B × 64] · [64 × 32]
  the inner numbers must match, and the outer ones give the shape of the result, [B × 32]. A cell of the result
  collects 64 products: the whole image weighted by one neuron. A column of the weight matrix
  is exactly one neuron, and there are 32 such columns.
</div>

<p>Let's see step by step how a batch turns into probabilities.</p>

    <button type="button" data-nav="prev">← Back</button>
    <button type="button" data-nav="next">Next →</button>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1" data-focus="x w1 b1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what is given</div>
      <h4>The batch and the first layer's parameters</h4>
<p>On the left is the matrix X: four images of 64 numbers each. Next to it are the first layer's parameters: a 64 × 32 weight matrix and a row of 32 biases. Yellow changes during training, green is recomputed from scratch on every batch, blue is data. A rectangle is larger the more rows and columns it has; where there are no more than ten, the cells are shown one by one. Above each matrix is its shape: rows × columns.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="X \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times 64},\quad W^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{64\times 32},\quad b^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{32}"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1 z1 dim1" data-focus="z1 dim1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · multiplication</div>
      <h4>Row times column gives 4 × 32</h4>
<p>The inner dimensions meet and cancel: [4 × 64] · [64 × 32] = [4 × 32]. A cell of the result is a sum of 64 products: one whole image weighted by one hidden neuron. Each column of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span> is an independent detector that looks at all 64 cells at once.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="Z^{(1)} = X\,W^{(1)} + b^{(1)} \qquad [4\times 64]\cdot[64\times 32] \rightarrow [4\times 32]"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1 z1 bc1" data-focus="b1 bc1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · bias</div>
      <h4>One row is added to every row of the batch</h4>
<p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(1)}"></span> is 32 numbers, and we add them to a 4 × 32 matrix. The row is copied to every example in the batch: the bias belongs to the neuron, not to the image. This is the only place where the shapes do not match literally, and it is worth keeping in mind: in the backward pass this copying will turn into summation.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="z^{(1)}_{ij} = \sum_{k=1}^{64} x_{ik}\, w^{(1)}_{kj} + b^{(1)}_{j}"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1 z1 h1 relu1" data-focus="h1 relu1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · ReLU</div>
      <h4>Negative values are zeroed, the shape does not change</h4>
<p>ReLU works element by element: cells do not mix. The shape stays 4 × 32, but roughly half of the cells become zeros. This is where the network stops being a linear function of the input, and this is where a mask of zeros and ones will appear in the backward pass.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="H^{(1)} = \max\left(0,\; Z^{(1)}\right) \qquad [4\times 32] \rightarrow [4\times 32]"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1 z1 h1 h1b w2 b2 z2 dim2" data-focus="h1b w2 b2 z2 dim2">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · second layer</div>
      <h4>The same trick again: 32 features → 10 scores</h4>
<p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="H^{(1)}"></span> becomes the input of the second layer, and everything repeats: [4 × 32] · [32 × 10] + [10] = [4 × 10]. The second layer does not know there was a first one before it: it just sees a matrix. This repeatability is what makes it possible to build networks of any depth.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="Z^{(2)} = H^{(1)} W^{(2)} + b^{(2)} \qquad [4\times 32]\cdot[32\times 10] \rightarrow [4\times 10]"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1 z1 h1 h1b w2 b2 z2 p soft" data-focus="p soft">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · softmax</div>
      <h4>Each row turns into ten probabilities</h4>
<p>Softmax is applied row by row: examples do not mix with each other. After it, each row has ten positive numbers that add up to exactly 1. The order is preserved: whichever score was larger has the larger probability. The shape is the same, 4 × 10, but the meaning changed: these are no longer scores but class probabilities.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="p_{ic} = e^{\,z^{(2)}_{ic}} \Big/ \sum_{c'=1}^{10} e^{\,z^{(2)}_{ic'}} \qquad \sum_c p_{ic} = 1"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="x w1 b1 z1 h1 h1b w2 b2 z2 p l lmark" data-focus="l lmark">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · loss</div>
      <h4>A 4 × 10 matrix and 4 × 10 labels collapse into one number</h4>
<p>The last step compares P with Y and outputs a single number, the batch loss. The whole forward pass is two matrix multiplications, two bias additions and two element-wise operations; there is nothing else in the network.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="L = -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{c} y_{ic}\,\log p_{ic}"></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>The shapes match for any batch size and any layer width. Check this on other numbers and see what NumPy does if you swap the factors.</p>

<div class="hn-live" id="wiShapes"></div>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the forward pass is two matrix multiplications and two element-wise
  operations. Multiplications change the shape and mix numbers together; ReLU and softmax keep the shape
  and work within a row. There is nothing third in the network.
</div>

---

## Part 7. The forward pass: the same steps in numbers

<p>
  Now let's plug in real numbers. The batch is the first four images of the first batch of the first epoch:
  the digits 3, 5, 2 and 8. The weights are drawn by a random number generator: a normal distribution with zero
  mean and standard deviation <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\sqrt{2/64} = 0.1768"></span>
  for the first layer and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\sqrt{2/32} = 0.25"></span> for the second.
  The biases are zeros.
</p>

<div class="callout-blue">
  <strong>Why the weights are random and the biases zero:</strong> if all weights were initialized to zero,
  all 32 neurons would compute the same thing and get the same gradient, and they would never
  diverge. Randomness is needed exactly to break this symmetry. The biases have nothing to break,
  so they are safely set to zero. The factor <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\sqrt{2/n_{\text{in}}}"></span>
  is chosen so that the spread of values neither grows nor fades from layer to layer.
</div>

<pre><code>def forward(X):
    Z1 = X @ W1 + b1
    H1 = np.maximum(Z1, 0)
    Z2 = H1 @ W2 + b2
    E = np.exp(Z2 - Z2.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return Z1, H1, Z2, E / E.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)</code></pre>

<p>
  Subtracting the maximum in softmax is a mandatory implementation detail: the exponential of a large number
  overflows, and subtracting a constant does not change the result, because it cancels
  in the numerator and the denominator.
</p>

<p>
  Next comes the arithmetic itself, cell by cell. The matrices below are drawn with indices: you can see
  which row is multiplied by which column and which cell of the result it lands in.
  There are no numbers inside the cells, since they would not fit, but they are plugged in
  in the description of each step, so any digit can be rechecked on a calculator.
</p>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e1" data-focus="e1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what is given</div>
      <h4>The batch is a 4 × 64 matrix, one row per image</h4>
<p>Row i is a whole image unfolded into 64 numbers; cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_{ik}"></span> is the brightness of point k divided by 16, so all values lie between 0 and 1. The first row is the three, then the five, the two and the eight.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="X \in \mathbb{R}^{4\times 64},\quad W^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{64\times 32},\quad b^{(1)} \in \mathbb{R}^{32}"></div>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} x_{1,1} = 0,\quad x_{1,2} = 0.0625,\quad x_{1,3} = 0.5,\quad x_{1,4} = 0.875, \\ x_{1,5} = 0.9375,\quad x_{1,6} = 0.125,\quad x_{1,7} = x_{1,8} = 0 \end{gathered}"></div><p>The first row has 34 nonzero numbers out of 64; the rest is background. This will matter in a step: an empty cell contributes nothing to any sum.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e1 h1" data-focus="h1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · one cell of the result</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="z^{(1)}_{1,22} = 1.0536"></span> is a sum of 64 products</h4>
<p>Highlighted are row 1 of the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span>, column 22 of the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(1)}"></span>, and the cell they produce. The rule is the same for all 128 cells: a cell of the result is the dot product of a row and a column.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="z^{(1)}_{1,22} = \sum_{k=1}^{64} x_{1k}\,w^{(1)}_{k,22}"></div><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} = 0.0625\cdot 0.1160 + 0.5\cdot 0.1114 + 0.875\cdot 0.1284 \\ + 0.9375\cdot 0.1909 + 0.125\cdot(-0.1844) + \ldots = 1.0536 \end{gathered}"></div><p>There are exactly 34 meaningful terms, one per nonempty pixel. The largest: 0.75 · 0.3459 = 0.2594, the most negative: 1 · (−0.1957) = −0.1957. The pluses add up to 1.75175, the minuses to −0.69815, and the difference is 1.0536.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e1 eb" data-focus="eb">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · bias</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(1)}"></span> is a row of 32 numbers, yet it is added to a 4 × 32 matrix</h4>
<p>The shapes do not match literally, and this is the only place in the forward pass where that happens: the same row of biases is added to all four rows, because the bias belongs to the neuron, not to the image. In the backward pass this copying will turn into summation over rows.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="z^{(1)}_{ij} = \sum_{k} x_{ik} w^{(1)}_{kj} + b^{(1)}_{j}, \qquad b^{(1)}_{22} = 0"></div><p>At the start all biases are zero, so right now <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(1)}"></span> consists entirely of products. After the very first descent step they will become nonzero, and that changes nothing in the formula.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e2" data-focus="e2">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · ReLU</div>
      <h4>56 cells out of 128 pass, 72 are zeroed</h4>
<p>ReLU acts cell by cell: the indices do not mix, the shape stays 4 × 32. A cell either passes as is or becomes zero.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="h^{(1)}_{1,22} = \max(0;\, 1.0536) = 1.0536, \qquad h^{(1)}_{1,21} = \max(0;\, -1.2744) = 0"></div><p>Per example, 12, 16, 12 and 16 neurons out of 32 are open. Ten neurons are closed for all four images at once: on this batch they take part neither in the answer nor, as we will see, in training.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e3 h3" data-focus="h3">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · second layer</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="z^{(2)}_{1,4} = 0.3139"></span> is the score of class “3”</h4>
<p>The same operation with different sizes: [4 × 32] · [32 × 10] = [4 × 10]. The second layer does not know there was a first one before it: it just sees a matrix of numbers.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} z^{(2)}_{1,4} = \sum_{j=1}^{32} h^{(1)}_{1j}\, w^{(2)}_{j,4} \\ = 0.7629\cdot(-0.1014) + 0.2729\cdot(-0.0436) + \ldots \\ + 1.0536\cdot 0.2681 + \ldots = 0.3139 \end{gathered}"></div><p>There are only 12 meaningful terms: the other 20 activations are zero after ReLU. The largest comes from neuron 22: 1.0536 · 0.2681 = 0.2825, and it is what pulled class “3” to the maximum of the row.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e4" data-focus="e4">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · softmax</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_{1,4} = 0.1488"></span>, and the whole row adds up to 1</h4>
<p>Softmax works within a row: examples do not mix. We divide the exponential of a cell by the sum of the ten exponentials of the same row.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="p_{1,4} = \dfrac{e^{0.3139}}{\sum_{c} e^{z^{(2)}_{1c}}} = \dfrac{1.3688}{9.1979} = 0.1488"></div><p>The whole first row: 0.0876; 0.0949; 0.0824; <strong>0.1488</strong>; 0.1185; 0.0890; 0.0579; 0.1244; 0.0918; 0.1046. No value has moved far from 0.1: the network honestly does not know the answer, and the maximum landed on the correct class by chance.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e5" data-focus="e5">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · loss</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="L = 2.1416"></span> against <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ln 10 = 2.3026"></span></h4>
<p>From each row of P exactly one cell is taken, the one where the correct class is. For our four images these are columns 4, 6, 3 and 9. The other 36 numbers do not enter the formula at all.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} L = -\tfrac{1}{4}\left(\log 0.1488 + \log 0.1381 + \log 0.1099 + \log 0.0843\right) \\ = \tfrac{1}{4}\left(1.9050 + 1.9796 + 2.2081 + 2.4735\right) = 2.1416 \end{gathered}"></div><p>The eight is penalized the most, 2.4735: it got the smallest probability, 0.0843. It is the one that will pull the gradient hardest.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>The scene computed one cell out of 128. The other 127 follow the same rule; pick any of them.</p>

<div class="hn-live" id="wiCell"></div>

<div class="callout-red">
  <strong>Careful with “it already guessed”:</strong> the untrained network named two images out of four correctly.
  This is not a sign that something works; it is chance on a sample of four examples.
  On the whole held-out set the same network gets 12.44%, almost exactly the guessing level.
</div>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> in an untrained network all ten probabilities are about 0.1,
  and the loss is close to ln 10 = 2.3026. This is the correct initial state and the best reference point at the start:
  if the first batches give a loss of about 2.3, all is well; if 20, there is a bug somewhere.
</div>

---

## Part 8. The loss: one number instead of forty

<p>
  The network outputs forty numbers: four examples with ten probabilities each. To compare states of the network
  with each other and to take derivatives, we need one number. It is given by <strong>cross-entropy</strong>: take
  the probability the network assigned to the correct class, compute its logarithm with a minus sign, and average
  over the batch.
</p>

### The error on one image

<p>
  Let's start with one image, the three from the batch, and compute the network's error on it. Classes here are numbered
  by the digits themselves, from 0 to 9.
</p>

<p>Let's see step by step how ten probabilities turn into one number.</p>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="p" data-focus="p"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · the network's answer</div><h4>Ten probabilities that sum to 1</h4><p>The forward pass from part 7 ended with softmax: the three has ten probabilities <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_0, \dots, p_9"></span>, one per digit. All of them are close to 0.1 because the weights are still random. The three got the most, 0.1488, but that is a coincidence: on all held-out images the same network is right 12.44% of the time.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="p yrow ideal" data-focus="yrow ideal"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · the correct answer</div><h4>The label is also a row of ten numbers</h4><p>The correct answer is known from the label: it is 3. To compare it with ten probabilities, the label is written in the same form, as a row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf y"></span> of ten numbers with 1 at the correct digit and 0 elsewhere. This encoding is called one-hot.</p><p>An ideal network would output <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbf p = \mathbf y"></span>: probability 1 for the three and 0 for the rest. Its answer is shown dashed.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="p yrow pen ref" data-focus="pen ref"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · penalty</div><h4>Each digit has its own penalty <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-\log p_c"></span></h4><p>For each digit we compute minus the logarithm of its probability (natural logarithm). The penalty shows how small the probability is: at 1 it is 0, at 0.5 it is 0.69, at 0.1 it is 2.30, at 0.01 it is 4.61.</p><p>So a confident mistake costs much more than an honest “I don't know”: probability 0.01 for the correct digit gives a penalty of 4.61, while 0.1 gives only 2.30. All of our three's probabilities are about 0.1, so the penalties are about 2.3 too: from 1.9050 for the three to 2.8486 for the six, which the network gave the least.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="p yrow pen fade prod col" data-focus="prod col fade"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · the label selects</div><h4>Of ten penalties, one gets into the error</h4><p>Each penalty is multiplied by the label of its digit. The nine wrong digits have label 0, and the product is zero whatever the probability. Only the three remains: 1 · 1.9050.</p><p>The network gave the six the least, 0.0579, but for the three this is not an error: its penalty of 2.8486 did not get into the sum.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="p yrow pen fade prod col ell" data-focus="ell"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · the image's error</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ell = -\log 0.1488 = 1.9050"></span></h4><p>The network's error on an image is the sum of ten “label × penalty” products:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\ell = -\sum_{c=0}^{9} y_c \log p_c = -\log p_3 = -\log 0.1488 = 1.9050"></div><p>Because the label is one-hot, the long sum always reduces to one term: minus the logarithm of the probability of the correct class.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="p yrow pen prod ell up" data-focus="p up"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · how to decrease it</div><h4>Raising <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_3"></span> means lowering the rest</h4><p>To decrease <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ell"></span>, the network needs to raise <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_3"></span>: at <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_3 = 1"></span> the error becomes zero. The probabilities of the other digits do not enter the formula, but they affect it through softmax:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="p_3 = \frac{e^{z_3}}{\sum_c e^{z_c}} = \frac{1.3688}{9.1979} = 0.1488"></div><p>The denominator is shared by all ten, so <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_3"></span> grows both when the score <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_3"></span> grows and when the scores of the other digits fall. The probabilities always add up to 1: if the three goes up, the other nine go down.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>You can check this by hand. Move the scores of one image and watch how the probabilities, the penalties of all ten digits and the error change. The gray penalties rise and fall, but only the red one gets into the error. The bottom row is the gradient with which the backward pass will start in part 9.</p>

<div class="hn-live" id="wiLogits"></div>

<p>
  The error of each image in the batch is computed the same way, only each has its own correct digit. The batch loss is
  their mean:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="L = -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{c} y_{ic}\,\log p_{ic} \;=\; -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} \log p_{i,\,y_i}"></div>

<p>
  The second equality is the same thing written more briefly: the one-hot label zeroes nine terms
  out of ten, and exactly one remains in the sum. Both forms are useful: the first is convenient for deriving the gradient,
  the second for understanding.
</p>

<p>For two classes the same loss is called log loss. Its derivation together with the sigmoid is covered in the article <a href="article.html?slug=logistic-regression-full-cycle">“Logistic regression: the full training cycle on four students”</a>.</p>

<p>Let's see step by step how one number comes out of forty.</p>

    <div class="step-panel" data-on="rows" data-focus="rows"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · four images</div><h4>Each image has its own correct digit</h4><p>The batch has four images: a three, a five, a two and an eight. Of each one's ten probabilities we need one, the one at its correct digit: 0.1488, 0.1381, 0.1099 and 0.0843. The other 36 numbers do not enter the loss.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="rows ells max" data-focus="ells max"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · four errors</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ell_i = -\log p_{\text{true}}"></span> for each image</h4><p>The error of each image is computed the same way as for the three above: minus the logarithm of the probability of its correct digit. The eight is penalized the most, 2.4735: it got the smallest probability, 0.0843. It will also pull the gradient harder than the others.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="rows ells mean" data-focus="mean"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · the mean</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="L = 2.1416"></span> is one number for the whole batch</h4><p>The batch loss is the mean of the four errors:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="L = \tfrac{1}{4}\left(1.9050 + 1.9796 + 2.2081 + 2.4735\right) = 2.1416"></div><p>Dividing by the batch size makes the loss comparable between batches of different sizes. The same division will appear in the first formula of the backward pass.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="rows ells mean scale" data-focus="scale"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · what to compare with</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ln 10 = 2.3026"></span> is the level of total ignorance</h4><p>If the network gives each of the ten digits 0.1, the error of every image is −log 0.1 = 2.3026, and so is the loss. Our 2.1416 is slightly lower: we were lucky with the initial weights. Zero is the ideal network, in which the probability of the correct digit is 1 on every image.</p><p>This is the best reference point at the start of training: a loss of about 2.3 means the network has learned nothing yet; a loss of 5 or 10 means a bug in the code or a step that is too large.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="rows ells mean scale train" data-focus="train"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · where we will end up</div><h4>0.5712 after the first epoch, 0.0266 after the thirtieth</h4><p>This is the path training will take (part 13): after the first epoch, that is, 42 steps, the loss is 0.5712, after the thirtieth it is 0.0266. These two numbers are averages not over our four images but over all 1347 training images, so they are green.</p><p>Everything further in the article is about how to move 2410 numbers so that this one number goes down.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

### What exactly we decrease

<p>
  The loss is a function not of the images but of the parameters. The images and labels are fixed, and only
  the 2410 numbers <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\theta = (W^{(1)}, b^{(1)}, W^{(2)}, b^{(2)})"></span> change. The goal of training is the mean loss over all
  1347 training images:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="L_{\text{train}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{1347}\sum_{n=1}^{1347} -\log p_{n,\,y_n}(\theta)"></div>

<p>
  At each step it is computed not over all images but over a batch: the mean over 32 images is an estimate of the same
  mean, only 42 times cheaper. In the running example the batch has four images, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="L = 2.1416"></span>.
</p>

<p>
  To decrease L, for each parameter we need to know: if it is increased a little, will the loss go up or
  down, and how fast. This is the derivative <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial \theta"></span>. Take the weight
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(2)}_{22,4}"></span> from neuron 22 to the output of the three: it affects L through the score <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z^{(2)}_{4}"></span>
  of each image, and that score affects all ten probabilities through softmax. A first-layer weight
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(1)}_{2,22}"></span> is one step further away: it changes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22}"></span>, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22}"></span> enters all ten scores.
</p>

<p>
  The derivative can be found head-on: shift the parameter by a small ε and recompute the loss. But that is one
  extra forward pass per parameter, 2410 passes per training step. The backward pass
  gets all 2410 derivatives in one pass over the graph from right to left: the derivative at each node
  is assembled from the already computed derivatives of the nodes to its right. This is the chain rule applied to the graph
  from part 2.
</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the loss is the single number the network decreases,
  and it is always worth keeping a reference point next to it. For ten classes that reference point is
  ln 10 = 2.3026: this is what a network that knows nothing gets.
</div>

---

## Part 9. The backward pass on the graph

<p>
  Let's go back to the graph from part 2. The forward pass went along the connections from left to right and left a number
  in each neuron. The backward pass goes along the same connections from right to left and leaves in each neuron
  a <strong>signal</strong> <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\delta"></span>, the derivative of the loss with respect to that neuron's sum, and on each connection
  the derivative with respect to its weight.
</p>

<p>
  There are two rules. The derivative with respect to a connection's weight equals the value at its input times the signal at its end.
  A neuron's signal is the sum of “connection weight × signal at the end” products over all connections leaving
  it, multiplied by the derivative of ReLU. We will derive them rigorously in part 10; here let's see how they
  work on the three.
</p>

<p>The rule itself, “walk along the arrows from the error to the parameter and multiply”, is covered in detail in the article <a href="article.html?slug=backprop">“Backpropagation: how to read a network from right to left”</a>.</p>

<p>Let's see step by step how the red signal travels from the loss to the first layer.</p>
