  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss" data-focus="loss"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what we look for</div><h4>The forward pass is done, now back along the same connections</h4><p>This is the graph from part 2 after the forward pass: the neurons are filled with their values, and the loss has been added on the right. For the three the penalty is −log 0.1488 = 1.9050, for the whole batch of four images <span class="math-inline" data-tex="L = 2.1416"></span>.</p><p>We need the derivative of L with respect to every connection and every bias: 2410 numbers. The backward pass gets them by moving from L to the left along the same connections. Below is everything for the first image of the batch; the contributions of the other three are computed the same way and added up.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss d2" data-focus="d2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · the signal at the output</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\delta^{(2)} = (\mathbf p - \mathbf y)/4"></span></h4><p>The first red step: how <span class="math-inline" data-tex="L"></span> changes if the score <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_c"></span> is shifted a little. For the softmax and cross-entropy pair the answer is “probability minus correct answer”, divided by the batch size (derived in part 10). The three's correct class is 3, so there <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(0.1488 - 1)/4 = -0.2128"></span>; for the others it is just <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_c/4"></span>, for example <span class="math-inline" data-tex="0.0876/4 = 0.0219"></span>.</p><p>The minus at the three means: increase this score and the loss will drop. The pluses at the others: their scores should be decreased.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss d2 g2" data-focus="g2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · second-layer weights</div><h4>A weight's derivative is the connection's input times the signal</h4><p>The weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(2)}_{jc}"></span> enters the score <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_c"></span> as the term <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j w^{(2)}_{jc}"></span>. If the weight is shifted by a small ε, the score shifts by <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j \varepsilon"></span>, and the loss by <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j \delta_c \varepsilon"></span>. So the derivative with respect to a connection's weight equals “value at its input × signal at its output”.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="\partial L/\partial w^{(2)}_{jc} = \textstyle\sum_{\text{images}} h_j\,\delta^{(2)}_c, \qquad \partial L/\partial b^{(2)}_c = \textstyle\sum_{\text{images}} \delta^{(2)}_c"></div>
<p>For the connection 22 → “3” the three's contribution is:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="h_{22}\,\delta_3 = 1.0536\cdot(-0.2128) = -0.2242"></div><p>The red connections are the largest of the 320 such products. The dashed neurons have no connections: they have <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j = 0"></span>, and the weights from them had no effect on this image. A bias's derivative is just the signal δ, because the bias enters the score with a factor of 1.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss d2 dh" data-focus="dh"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · the signal into a hidden neuron</div><h4>A neuron collects signals from all the outputs it feeds</h4><p>The value <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{22}"></span> enters all ten scores, each time with its own weight. So its derivative is the sum of ten “connection weight × signal at its end” contributions. The red arrows go along the same ten connections as in the forward pass, only in the opposite direction.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_{22}} = \sum_{c} w^{(2)}_{22,c}\,\delta_c = 0.2681\cdot(-0.2128) + (-0.1697)\cdot 0.0219 + \ldots \\ = -0.0661 \end{gathered}"></div><p>The main contribution, −0.0570, comes from the connection to the correct class. The signal of each of the 32 neurons is computed the same way.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss d2 mask" data-focus="mask"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · through ReLU</div><h4>The signal passes only through open neurons</h4><p>In the forward pass ReLU let positive sums through and zeroed the rest. Backward it is the same: for an open neuron a small shift of the sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_j"></span> shifts <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j"></span> by the same amount, for a closed one it does not shift it at all. So <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\delta^{(1)}_j"></span> equals the signal from step 4 for the 12 open neurons and zero for the 20 closed ones.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="\delta^{(1)}_j = \partial L/\partial h_j \cdot \mathbb 1\left[z^{(1)}_j > 0\right]"></div>
<p>For neuron 22, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\delta^{(1)}_{22} = -0.0661"></span>. The saturation of red shows the size of the signal; the strongest are at neurons 15 and 16: −0.1015 and 0.1021.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss d2 mask g1" data-focus="g1"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · first-layer weights</div><h4>The same rule: connection input × signal</h4><p>The weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(1)}_{kj}"></span> connects cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_k"></span> to neuron <span class="math-inline" data-tex="j"></span>, so its derivative is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_k\,\delta^{(1)}_j"></span>. The formula is the same as for the second layer: a layer does not know its number.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="\partial L/\partial w^{(1)}_{kj} = \textstyle\sum_{\text{images}} x_k\,\delta^{(1)}_j, \qquad \partial L/\partial b^{(1)}_j = \textstyle\sum_{\text{images}} \delta^{(1)}_j"></div>
<p>For the connection from cell 2 to neuron 22 the three's contribution is:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="x_2\,\delta_{22} = 0.0625\cdot(-0.0661) = -0.0041"></div><p>Red connections leave only inked cells and enter only open neurons. An empty cell gives zero for any signal, a closed neuron gives zero for any image. On this three, 34 · 12 = 408 of the 2048 first-layer derivatives are nonzero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="img flat net loss mask g1 g2 d2" data-focus="g1 g2 d2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · from the graph to matrices</div><h4>All red connections of a layer are one matrix multiplication</h4><p>Put the derivative for each connection <span class="math-inline" data-tex="j \to c"></span> into cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(j, c)"></span>, like the weights in part 3. This gives a 32 × 10 table of products <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_j\,\delta_c"></span>: a column of neuron values times a row of signals, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(\mathbf h^{(1)})^{\top} \delta^{(2)}"></span>.</p><p>For a batch of four images the contributions add up. For the connection 22 → “3” the three's contribution is −0.2242, while for the five, the two and the eight the three is a wrong class, their output signal is positive, and so are their contributions: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-0.2242 + 0.0197 + 0.0165 + 0.0276 = -0.1604"></span>. The sum over images is exactly the matrix multiplication <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(H^{(1)})^{\top} \cdot \partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span>. For both layers:</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(2)} = (H^{(1)})^{\top}\,\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}, \qquad \partial L/\partial W^{(1)} = X^{\top}\,\partial L/\partial Z^{(1)}"></div>
<p>Next we derive these formulas rigorously and compute them with matrices.</p>
</div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the backward pass goes along the same connections as the forward one. On a connection
  the derivative equals “connection input × signal at its end”; a neuron's signal is collected from all connections
  leaving it and is zeroed for neurons closed by ReLU.
</div>

---

## Part 10. The backward pass: deriving five formulas

<p>
  On the graph in part 9 the rules of the backward pass appeared as observations. Now let's derive them rigorously,
  from the definition of the derivative and the chain rule, and write them with matrices for the whole batch at once. The backward
  pass gives all 2410 derivatives in one pass from right to left and costs about as much
  as the forward one.
</p>

<p>
  One convention without which the derivation sprawls. The derivative of a scalar with respect to a matrix is a matrix
  of the same shape, whose cell holds the derivative with respect to the corresponding number:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}\right)_{jc} \;=\; \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{jc}}"></div>

<p>
  This immediately gives the shape rule we will use as a check: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> has
  shape 64 × 32, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial b^{(2)}"></span> is ten numbers, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span> is 4 × 10. Below are three derivations: softmax
  with cross-entropy, the linear layer and ReLU. There is nothing else in our network.
</p>

<p>The same derivations for a network with several hidden layers are in the article <a href="article.html?slug=mlp-full-cycle">“A fully connected neural network from scratch”</a>, and one full training step of such a network on one canvas is on the <a href="article.html?slug=mlp-map">map of a fully connected network</a>.</p>

### Derivation 1. Softmax and cross-entropy give P − Y

<p>The whole backward pass starts with this derivation. Let's work through it on the three, one derivative per step.</p>

<g data-key="res1" data-only="1"><foreignObject x="708" y="116" width="230" height="60"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:26px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\displaystyle = p_y - 1"></span></span></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="714" y="174" width="230" height="20"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:12px;color:#D83BB9;font-weight:700"><span><span data-tex="p_y"></span>&nbsp;cancelled · case&nbsp;<span data-tex="m = y"></span></span></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="714" y="197" width="220" height="22"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:12.5px;color:#5E5850;font-weight:400"><span>the three:&nbsp;<span data-tex="-0.8512"></span></span></div></foreignObject></g>
<g data-key="res2" data-only="1"><foreignObject x="708" y="116" width="230" height="60"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:26px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\displaystyle = p_m"></span></span></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="714" y="174" width="230" height="20"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:12px;color:#D83BB9;font-weight:700"><span><span data-tex="p_y"></span>&nbsp;cancelled · case&nbsp;<span data-tex="m \ne y"></span></span></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="714" y="197" width="220" height="22"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:12.5px;color:#5E5850;font-weight:400"><span>zero on the three:&nbsp;<span data-tex="0.0876"></span></span></div></foreignObject></g>
<g data-key="final" data-only="1"><rect x="30" y="488" width="900" height="58" rx="10" fill="#FDF2FB" stroke="#D83BB9" stroke-width="1.6"/><foreignObject x="48" y="488" width="860" height="58"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:21px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\displaystyle \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_m} = p_m - y_m \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z^{(2)}} = \frac{P - Y}{B}"></span></span></div></foreignObject></g>
<text x="30" y="560" font-size="12.5" fill="#5E5850">red is what is already known or came from the right · blue is the derivative inside this block · magenta is the result</text>

  <div class="stage-bar">
    <button type="button" data-nav="prev">← Back</button>
    <button type="button" data-nav="next">Next →</button>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given hg base rq bq" data-focus="given hg"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what is given</div><h4>Two formulas from the end of the forward pass</h4><p>The “given” line is the last two actions of the forward pass from parts 7 and 8, written for one image.</p><p><strong>Softmax.</strong> The second layer output ten scores <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_0, \dots, z_9"></span>, one per digit. Softmax exponentiates each and divides by the sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="S"></span> of all ten exponentials. This gives the probabilities <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_c"></span>: all positive, summing to 1. For the three <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_3 = 0.3139"></span>, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="S = 9.1979"></span>, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_3 = e^{0.3139}/9.1979 = 1.3688/9.1979 = 0.1488"></span>.</p><p><strong>The image's error</strong> from part 8: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ell = -\sum_c y_c \log p_c"></span>. The label <span class="math-inline" data-tex="y_c"></span> equals 1 only at the correct class, so one term remains of the sum: minus the logarithm of the probability of the correct class. Denote the number of the correct class <span class="math-inline" data-tex="y"></span>: for the three <span class="math-inline" data-tex="y = 3"></span> and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ell = -\log 0.1488 = 1.9050"></span>.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base rq bq" data-focus="rq bq"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · what we look for</div><h4>The derivative is a product of two factors</h4><p>We look for <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial\ell/\partial z_m"></span>: how the error changes if one score <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_m"></span> is shifted a little. There are ten such derivatives.</p><p>The error depends only on <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span>, so a score acts on it along one path: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_m"></span> changes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span>, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> changes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\ell"></span>. By the chain rule the derivative is a product of two factors. These are two empty slots: red and blue. Below we find what to put in them.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base rq bq rcard" data-focus="rcard"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · the red card</div><h4>How the error depends on the probability</h4><p>The error is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-\log p_y"></span>, and the derivative <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-\log x"></span> equals <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-1/x"></span>. Substitute <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> for <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x"></span>.</p><p>On the three, −1/0.1488 = −6.7197: if the probability of the three grows by a small ε, the error falls by 6.7197 ε.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bq rcard rfill rarr" data-focus="rfill rarr"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · into the red slot</div><h4>Putting what we found into the formula</h4><p>The red factor is found; move it up: the first factor is now <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-1/p_y"></span>. The blue slot is still empty: its value depends on whose score we move, its own or another one.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bq rcard rfill bcard brow1 bsel1" data-focus="brow1 bsel1"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · the blue card, own score</div><h4>Case <span class="math-inline" data-tex="m = y"></span></h4><p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> is the fraction <span class="math-inline" data-tex="e^{z_y}/S"></span>, and its own score <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_y"></span> appears on both floors: in the numerator and as one of the terms in <span class="math-inline" data-tex="S"></span>. The quotient rule: derivative of the numerator times the denominator minus the numerator times the derivative of the denominator, all over the square of the denominator.</p><p>Both derivatives equal <span class="math-inline" data-tex="e^{z_y}"></span>. Divide by <span class="math-inline" data-tex="S^2"></span> and recognize <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> itself in <span class="math-inline" data-tex="e^{z_y}/S"></span>: this gives <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y - p_y^2 = p_y(1 - p_y)"></span>.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bq rcard rfill bcard brow1 brow2 bsel2" data-focus="brow2 bsel2"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · the blue card, another score</div><h4>Case <span class="math-inline" data-tex="m \ne y"></span></h4><p>Another class's score is not in the numerator, so its derivative is 0. The denominator has the term <span class="math-inline" data-tex="e^{z_m}"></span>, whose derivative is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="e^{z_m}"></span>. By the same quotient rule what remains is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-e^{z_y}e^{z_m}/S^2"></span>, that is, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-p_y\,p_m"></span>.</p><p>The minus sign: by raising another class's score, the network increases the denominator and takes probability away from the correct class.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base rcard rfillc bcard brow1 brow2 bsel1 bfill1 barr1 res1" data-focus="bfill1 barr1 res1 rfillc"><div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · substituting, own score</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> cancels: what remains is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y - 1"></span></h4><p>Put the result of the own-score case into the blue slot. Now <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> stands in the denominator of the red factor and as a factor in the blue one: they cancel, and these are the struck-out places.</p><p>What remains is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-(1 - p_y) = p_y - 1"></span>. On the three, 0.1488 − 1 = −0.8512.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base rcard rfillc bcard brow1 brow2 bsel2 bfill2 barr2 res2" data-focus="bfill2 barr2 res2 rfillc"><div class="step-kicker">Step 8 · substituting, another score</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> cancels again: what remains is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_m"></span></h4><p>Now put the result of the other-score case into the blue slot. <span class="math-inline" data-tex="p_y"></span> cancels the same way, and the two minuses give a plus: what remains is just the probability of that other digit.</p><p>For zero on the three this is 0.0876.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base rcard rfill bcard brow1 brow2 final" data-focus="final"><div class="step-kicker">Step 9 · one formula</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial\ell/\partial z_m = p_m - y_m"></span></h4><p>The two cases differ only by the subtracted one, and it stands exactly where the label <span class="math-inline" data-tex="y_m = 1"></span> is. So this is one formula: “what the network output minus what was needed”. The sum over all scores is zero: the probabilities add up to 1, and so does the label.</p><p>The batch loss is the mean over <span class="math-inline" data-tex="B"></span> images, so each row is also divided by <span class="math-inline" data-tex="B"></span>, and the rows stack into a matrix. On the three with <span class="math-inline" data-tex="B = 4"></span>: −0.8512/4 = −0.2128 and 0.0876/4 = 0.0219, the first row of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span> in the second scene of this part.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>The result of the derivation for the whole batch:</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="\boxed{\;\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z^{(2)}} = \frac{P - Y}{B}\;} \qquad [B \times 10]"></div>

### Derivation 2. The linear layer: three derivatives from one formula

<p>The same technique for the linear layer: the red slot comes from derivation 1, the blue one is the derivative of the sum the layer computes.</p>

<g data-key="mb" data-only="1"><rect x="30" y="488" width="900" height="58" rx="10" fill="#FDF2FB" stroke="#D83BB9" stroke-width="1.6"/><foreignObject x="48" y="488" width="400" height="58"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:21px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\displaystyle \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \text{sum of } \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z} \text{ over rows}"></span></span></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="470" y="506" width="450" height="22"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:12.5px;color:#5E5850;font-weight:400"><span>bias “3”:&nbsp;<span data-tex="-0.2128 + 0.0339 + 0.0309 + 0.0290 = -0.1190"></span></span></div></foreignObject></g>
<g data-key="mh" data-only="1"><rect x="30" y="488" width="900" height="58" rx="10" fill="#FDF2FB" stroke="#D83BB9" stroke-width="1.6"/><foreignObject x="48" y="488" width="300" height="58"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:21px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\displaystyle \frac{\partial L}{\partial H} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z}\,W^{\top}"></span></span></div></foreignObject><foreignObject x="380" y="506" width="540" height="22"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:12.5px;color:#5E5850;font-weight:400"><span>neuron 22 on the three:&nbsp;<span data-tex="0.2681\cdot(-0.2128) + \ldots = -0.0661"></span></span></div></foreignObject></g>
<g data-key="mall" data-only="1"><rect x="30" y="488" width="900" height="58" rx="10" fill="#FDF2FB" stroke="#D83BB9" stroke-width="1.6"/><foreignObject x="48" y="488" width="860" height="58"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:20px;color:#111111;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\displaystyle \frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = H^{\top}\frac{\partial L}{\partial Z},\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \textstyle\sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_i},\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial H} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial Z}\,W^{\top}"></span></span></div></foreignObject></g>
<text x="30" y="560" font-size="12.5" fill="#5E5850">red is what is already known or came from the right · blue is the derivative inside this block · magenta is the result</text>

    <button type="button" data-nav="prev">← Back</button>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given hg base lw bq" data-focus="given hg"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what is given</div><h4>The second layer's formula written out for one number</h4><p>The “given” line is the second layer from parts 3 and 6, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z = HW + b"></span>, written for one cell of the result. The indices: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> is the image number in the batch, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="j"></span> is the hidden neuron number (from 1 to 32), <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span> is the class number (the column, from 1 to 10).</p><p>Cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_{ic}"></span> is the score of class <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span> on image <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span>. It is the dot product of row <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> of the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H"></span> (the values of the 32 hidden neurons on this image) and column <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span> of the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W"></span> (the 32 weights leading into class <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span>), plus the class bias <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b_c"></span>.</p><p>For example, the score of class “3” for the three (part 7, step 5): <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_{1,4} = 0.7629\cdot(-0.1014) + \ldots + 1.0536\cdot 0.2681 + \ldots = 0.3139"></span>. The first layer works the same way, only <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span> stands in place of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H"></span>.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base lw bq" data-focus="base lw"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · what we look for</div><h4>A weight affects the loss through every row of the batch</h4><p>The layer computes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_{ic} = \sum_j h_{ij} w_{jc} + b_c"></span>. The red slot is already filled: derivation 1 gave how the loss depends on the layer's output. We need the derivatives with respect to three kinds of numbers: the weight, the bias and the layer's input.</p><p>Start with the weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w_{jc}"></span>. It appears in the output <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_{ic}"></span> of every image in the batch, so its contribution to the loss is collected over all rows <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span>: the product is preceded by a sum over <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span>.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base lw bcard bw sbw fw aw rw" data-focus="bw sbw fw aw rw"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · the blue card: weight</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial z_{ic}/\partial w_{jc} = h_{ij}"></span></h4><p>In the sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\sum_j h_{ij} w_{jc}"></span> the weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w_{jc}"></span> appears in one term, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij} w_{jc}"></span>. The derivative of this term with respect to the weight is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij}"></span>; for the others it is zero. Put <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij}"></span> into the blue slot.</p><p>The derivative with respect to a connection's weight is “value at its input × signal at its output”, the same rule as on the graph in part 9.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base lw bcard bw fw rw mw" data-focus="mw"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · as a matrix</div><h4>The sum over <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> is a matrix multiplication</h4><p>A sum over a shared index <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> is the definition of the matrix product. In <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H"></span> the index <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> runs along the rows, so <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H"></span> is transposed, and all 320 derivatives are computed with one multiplication <span class="math-inline" data-tex="H^{\top}\,\partial L/\partial Z"></span>.</p><p>For the weight from neuron 22 to class “3”: 1.0536 · (−0.2128) + 0.5808 · 0.0339 + 0.5335 · 0.0309 + 0.9531 · 0.0290 = −0.1604. The sign is set by the first term: there the neuron was most active and the class was most wrong.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base lb bcard bw bb sbb fb ab rb mb" data-focus="lb bb sbb fb ab rb mb"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · bias</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial z_{ic}/\partial b_c = 1"></span></h4><p>The bias <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b_c"></span> enters every output <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_{ic}"></span> with a factor of 1. Put 1 into the blue slot: what remains of the product is just the sum of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial z_{ic}"></span> over the images, that is, the column sum.</p><p>In the forward pass the row of biases was copied to every row of the batch; in the backward pass the copying turns into a sum. For class “3”: −0.2128 + 0.0339 + 0.0309 + 0.0290 = −0.1190.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base lh bcard bw bb bh sbh fh ah rh mh" data-focus="lh bh sbh fh ah rh mh"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · the layer's input</div><h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial z_{ic}/\partial h_{ij} = w_{jc}"></span></h4><p>To go further left we need the derivative with respect to the layer's input <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij}"></span>. It stands in the same term <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij} w_{jc}"></span>, and its derivative with respect to <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij}"></span> is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w_{jc}"></span>. But <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij}"></span> enters all ten outputs of its row, so the sum is now over the classes <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span>.</p><p>The sum over <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span> is again a matrix multiplication, only now <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W"></span> is transposed: the same weight that carried the number forward carries the signal back. For neuron 22 on the three the main term is 0.2681 · (−0.2128) = −0.0570, and the whole sum is −0.0661.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base lw bcard bw bb bh mall" data-focus="mall bcard"><div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · three formulas</div><h4>One scheme, three derivatives</h4><p>All three come from one move: take the red slot from the right, put the derivative of the sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z"></span> with respect to the needed number into the blue slot, and add up the contributions over the index that is absent from the answer. Transposition puts that index in the place of the shared dimension: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> for the weights, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="c"></span> for the layer's input.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

### Derivation 3. ReLU is a mask

<p>The last link: the signal passes through ReLU. The red slot comes from derivation 2.</p>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given hg base bq" data-focus="given hg"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what is given</div><h4>ReLU between the layers</h4><p>The “given” line is ReLU from parts 2 and 6. It stands between the layers and acts on each cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(1)}"></span> separately: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="i"></span> is the image number, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="j"></span> is the hidden neuron number. A negative sum turns into zero, a positive one passes as is.</p><p>For the three (part 7, step 4): neuron 22 has the sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z = 1.0536"></span>, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h = 1.0536"></span>; neuron 21 has the sum <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z = -1.2744"></span>, and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h = 0"></span>. In total, on the batch 56 cells out of 128 passed and 72 were zeroed.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bq" data-focus="base"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · what we look for</div><h4>The signal before ReLU from the signal after it</h4><p>Between the layers stands <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij} = \max(0, z_{ij})"></span>. The red slot is already filled: derivation 2 gave how the loss depends on ReLU's output. What remains is the blue slot, how ReLU's output depends on its input.</p><p>There is no sum here, unlike derivation 2: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h_{ij}"></span> depends only on its own <span class="math-inline" data-tex="z_{ij}"></span>, since ReLU does not mix numbers together.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bq bcard" data-focus="bcard"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · the blue card</div><h4>The slope of ReLU is 0 or 1</h4><p>ReLU is two straight lines: horizontal to the left of zero and at 45° to the right. The horizontal one has slope 0, the slanted one slope 1, so the derivative takes only two values. It is written as <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbb 1[z > 0]"></span>: one if the condition holds, zero if not.</p><p>At zero itself there is no derivative, and that does not matter: in practice 0 or 1 is taken by convention, and hitting exactly zero happens with probability zero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bcard fill arr" data-focus="fill arr"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · into the blue slot</div><h4>The signal is multiplied by 0 or 1</h4><p>Put <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\mathbb 1[z_{ij} > 0]"></span> into the blue slot. For an open neuron the signal passes unchanged, for a closed one it is zeroed. The mask of zeros and ones was already computed in the forward pass: it is the sign of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(1)}"></span>.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bcard fill ex" data-focus="ex"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · on the three</div><h4>An open neuron passes, a closed one zeroes</h4><p>Neuron 22 on the three was open, its sum 1.0536 is positive: the signal −0.0661 passes as is. Neuron 21 is closed, its sum is −1.2744: the signal 0.0490 is multiplied by zero. Across the batch 72 cells out of 128 are zeroed this way.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="given base bcard fill mat" data-focus="mat"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · as a matrix</div><h4>The mask is multiplied cell by cell</h4><p>For the whole batch this is element-wise multiplication of the signal matrix by the mask: each cell is multiplied by its own. The sign <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\odot"></span> distinguishes it from the matrix product in derivation 2.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<div class="callout-yellow">
  <strong>This is where “dying” neurons come from:</strong> if a neuron is closed on all images of the batch,
  its column of the mask is all zeros: the gradient does not reach its weights, and they do not change.
  On our batch this is 10 neurons out of 32, and by the end of training two neurons will be closed
  on all 1347 images.
</div>

### All together

<p>
  The three derivations give five formulas, and two of them are applied twice, once per layer. Below is the full
  backward pass of our network; no sixth formula exists.
</p>

<table class="shape-table">
  <tr><th>Step</th><th>Formula</th><th>Shape</th></tr>
  <tr><td>input of the backward pass</td><td><code>(P − Y) / B</code></td><td>B × 10</td></tr>
  <tr><td>weight gradient</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="(\text{layer input})^{\top} \cdot (\text{output gradient})"></span></td><td>same as <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W"></span></td></tr>
  <tr><td>bias gradient</td><td>sum of the output gradient over rows</td><td>same as b</td></tr>
  <tr><td>passing back</td><td><span class="math-inline" data-tex="(\text{output gradient}) \cdot W^{\top}"></span></td><td>same as the layer input</td></tr>
  <tr><td>through ReLU</td><td>multiply by the mask <code>Z &gt; 0</code></td><td>unchanged</td></tr>
</table>

<p>
  Why this is cheap: each quantity is computed exactly once and reused further on.
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span> is needed both for the second-layer weights and for passing to the left; <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial H^{(1)}"></span> only to get
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(1)}"></span>, and that only to get the first-layer weights. No quantity is recomputed,
  so the whole backward pass costs about as much as one forward pass, not 2410 of them.
</p>

<p>Let's see step by step how the gradient travels from the loss to the first layer.</p>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="net gp hl4" data-focus="hl4">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what we look for</div>
      <h4>2410 derivatives, one per parameter</h4>
<p>We need to know how L changes under a tiny shift of each of the 2410 numbers. Computing this by definition takes 2410 separate forward passes. The backward pass gets all the derivatives at once in one pass from right to left, because along the way it reuses what has already been computed.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="net gp gz2 hl3" data-focus="gz2">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · the first node</div>
      <h4>Softmax and cross-entropy collapse into <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(P - Y)/B"></span></h4>
<p>Computed honestly, the derivative of the loss with respect to <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(2)}"></span> is the gradient of the loss with respect to <span class="math-inline" data-tex="P"></span> times the 10 × 10 Jacobian of softmax. But for the “softmax + cross-entropy” pair everything cancels down to the difference “what the network output minus what was needed”, divided by the batch size. So the red arrow passes straight through softmax, and the first real node is already <span class="math-inline" data-tex="Z^{(2)}"></span>.</p>
<div class="math-display" data-tex="\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial Z^{(2)}} = \dfrac{P - Y}{B} \qquad [4 \times 10]"></div>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="net gp gz2 gw2 hl2" data-focus="gw2">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · second-layer parameters</div>
      <h4>A weight's gradient is the input times the output gradient</h4>
<p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(2)} = (H^{(1)})^{\top} \cdot \partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span>: [32 × 4] · [4 × 10] = [32 × 10], the shape matches <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(2)}"></span> itself. The meaning is simple: the weight between neuron j and class c is to blame the more, the more active the neuron was and the more wrong the class was. For a bias the input is one, so there it is just the sum over the rows of the batch.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="net gp gz2 gw2 ga1 hl2" data-focus="ga1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · pushing back</div>
      <h4>The same weight, but transposed</h4>
<p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial H^{(1)} = \partial L/\partial Z^{(2)} \cdot (W^{(2)})^{\top}"></span>: [4 × 10] · [10 × 32] = [4 × 32]. Forward, the weight multiplied the input; backward, the same weight multiplies the gradient, only from the other side. Transposing is needed because <span class="math-inline" data-tex="W^{(2)}"></span> has shape 32 × 10, and a 4 × 10 gradient can only be multiplied by a matrix with ten rows.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="net gp gz2 gw2 ga1 gz1 hl1" data-focus="gz1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · through ReLU</div>
      <h4>A mask of zeros and ones</h4>
<p>The derivative of max(0, z) is 1 where z was positive and 0 elsewhere. So <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(1)} = \partial L/\partial H^{(1)} \odot [Z^{(1)} &gt; 0]"></span> is element-wise multiplication by the mask saved from the forward pass. ReLU lives inside the hidden layer's card, and the gradient passes straight through it, losing exactly the cells that were closed.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="net gp gz2 gw2 ga1 gz1 gw1 hl1" data-focus="gw1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · first-layer parameters</div>
      <h4>Exactly the same formula as for the second</h4>
<p><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)} = X^{\top} \cdot \partial L/\partial Z^{(1)}"></span>: [64 × 4] · [4 × 32] = [64 × 32]. The formula is the same as for the second layer, only the layer's input is now <span class="math-inline" data-tex="X"></span>: a layer does not know its number. This is why the backward pass is written as one loop over the layers in reverse order.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>
  The shapes match; now the same five formulas in cells and numbers. The matrices again have indices, but
  what travels through them is derivatives; at each step we compute one cell by hand and check it against
  what the code produced.
</p>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm0 e2 h2" data-focus="h2">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · input of the backward pass</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial z^{(2)}_{1,4} = (0.1488 - 1) / 4 = -0.2128"></span></h4>
<p>The “softmax + cross-entropy” pair collapses into the difference “what the network output minus what was needed”, divided by the batch size. The correct class gets one subtracted, the others zero.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}_{1,4}} = \dfrac{0.1488 - 1}{4} = -0.2128, \qquad \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}_{1,1}} = \dfrac{0.0876 - 0}{4} = 0.0219"></div><p>The whole first row: 0.0219; 0.0237; 0.0206; <strong>−0.2128</strong>; 0.0296; 0.0223; 0.0145; 0.0311; 0.0229; 0.0262. The row sums to exactly zero: the sum of all p is one, and so is the sum of all y.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm1 e3 h3" data-focus="h3">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · second-layer weight gradient</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial w^{(2)}_{22,4} = -0.1604"></span></h4>
<p>The weight between neuron 22 and class “3” took part in four outputs, one per image. The contributions add up, and each equals “activation × output gradient”.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w^{(2)}_{22,4}} = 1.0536\cdot(-0.2128) + 0.5808\cdot 0.0339 \\ + 0.5335\cdot 0.0309 + 0.9531\cdot 0.0290 \end{gathered}"></div><div class="math-display" data-tex="= -0.2242 + 0.0197 + 0.0165 + 0.0276 = -0.1604"></div><p>The first term sets the sign of the whole sum: where the neuron was most active, the class was most wrong. The minus means “increase this weight and the loss will drop”.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm2 e4 h4" data-focus="h4">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · bias gradient</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial b^{(2)}_{4} = -0.1190"></span> is just the column sum</h4>
<p>In the forward pass the bias was copied across the rows of the batch. The inverse of copying is summation: we add up column <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span> over all four examples.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial b^{(2)}_{4}} = -0.2128 + 0.0339 + 0.0309 + 0.0290 = -0.1190"></div><p>The whole row: 0.1076; 0.0868; −0.1736; −0.1190; 0.0993; −0.1269; 0.0648; 0.1207; −0.1605; 0.1007. They sum to zero, because every row of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span> summed to zero. The biases will not shift all ten scores at once; they change only the differences between classes.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm3 e5 h5" data-focus="h5">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · pushing the gradient left</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial h^{(1)}_{1,22} = -0.0661"></span></h4>
<p>The activation of neuron 22 took part in all ten scores of its row, each time with a weight as a factor. So we add up ten “weight × score gradient” products.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial h^{(1)}_{1,22}} = \sum_{c=1}^{10} w^{(2)}_{22,c}\,\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(2)}_{1c}} \\ = -0.2128\cdot 0.2681 + 0.0219\cdot(-0.0172) + \ldots = -0.0661 \end{gathered}"></div><p>The main term is the correct class: −0.2128 · 0.2681 = −0.0570. The same weight that carried the number forward carries the gradient back, only now the matrix is transposed.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm4 e6 h6" data-focus="h6">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · the ReLU mask</div>
      <h4>72 cells out of 128 are zeroed</h4>
<p>The derivative of max(0, z) is one where z was positive and zero elsewhere. So the mask taken in the forward pass is simply multiplied cell by cell.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(1)}_{1,22}} = -0.0661\cdot 1 = -0.0661, \qquad \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial z^{(1)}_{1,21}} = 0.0490\cdot 0 = 0"></div><p>This is where “dying” neurons live: ten neurons have a zero mask on all four images, and the gradient simply does not reach their weights.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm5 e7 h7" data-focus="h7">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · first-layer gradient</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial w^{(1)}_{2,22} = 0.0050"></span>, the same formula as for the second</h4>
<p>The formula is the same as for the second layer: the layer's input is transposed and multiplied by the output gradient. For the first layer the input is the images themselves.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w^{(1)}_{2,22}} = 0.0625\cdot(-0.0661) + 0\cdot(-0.0297) \\ + 0.1875\cdot 0.0486 + 0\cdot(-0.0491) \\ = -0.0041 + 0.0091 = 0.0050 \end{gathered}"></div><p>Two of the four images have zero in this pixel and contribute nothing at all. If a pixel is empty in all four, the whole row of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> is zero; on our batch there are 18 such rows out of 64. The biases are computed the same way as in the second layer: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial b^{(1)}_{22} = -0.0661 - 0.0297 + 0.0486 - 0.0491 = -0.0963"></span>.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="e1 ok" data-focus="ok">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · checking by shapes</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="2048 + 32 + 320 + 10 = 2410"></span>: everything matches</h4>
<p>The most useful check in practice: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> must have shape 64 × 32, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial b^{(2)}"></span> ten numbers, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(2)}"></span> 4 × 10. If the shapes match, the chance of an error in the derivation drops sharply; if not, the error is found before you even start computing.</p><p>To the left of the first layer a gradient exists too, <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial X"></span> of shape 4 × 64, but there is no reason to compute it: there are no parameters behind it. All 2410 numbers below are checked with central differences; the worst discrepancy is 3.7 · <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-11}"></span>.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> a gradient always has the shape of what we differentiate with respect to,
  and the same weight works forward and backward, only transposed in the second case.
  These two rules are enough to reconstruct the backward pass of any fully connected network from memory.
</div>

---

## Part 11. The backward pass in numbers and a gradient check

<p>
  The whole backward pass of our network is five lines of code. Note that nothing appears in them
  that was not in the forward pass: they use the saved <code>Z1</code>,
  <code>H1</code>, <code>P</code> and the weights themselves.
</p>

<pre><code>dZ2 = (P - Yb) / len(idx)
dW2, db2 = H1.T @ dZ2, dZ2.sum(0)
dZ1 = (dZ2 @ W2.T) * (Z1 > 0)
dW1, db1 = Xb.T @ dZ1, dZ1.sum(0)</code></pre>

<p>
  Writing these lines is easy, and getting them wrong is even easier: a mixed-up transpose or
  a forgotten division by the batch size will not raise any error; the network will just learn worse
  or not at all. So the only reliable check is numerical. We shift each parameter
  by ±ε, recompute the loss twice and compare with what the backward pass produced.
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta} \;\approx\; \frac{L(\theta + \varepsilon) - L(\theta - \varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon}, \qquad \varepsilon = 10^{-5}"></div>

<div class="callout-yellow">
  <strong>Where the numerical check honestly breaks:</strong> ReLU has a kink at zero. If ε is taken
  too large, the point <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\theta + \varepsilon"></span> can
  land on the other side of the kink; then the difference computes the derivative of a different function,
  and the discrepancy grows by orders of magnitude without any bug in the code. For ε = <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-5}"></span> this does not happen,
  but the effect is worth keeping in mind: safe values of ε lie between <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-6}"></span> and <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-4}"></span>.
</div>

<p>The check can be repeated for any parameter. Move ε and see at which values the differences stop matching the backward pass.</p>

<div class="hn-live" id="wiCheck"></div>

<p>Let's see what the first-layer gradient looks like if each of its columns is folded back into an 8 × 8 image.</p>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="imgs sig" data-focus="sig"><div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · signals</div><h4>The signal of neuron 22 on each of the four images</h4><p>The backward pass has already reached the hidden layer and computed the signal of every neuron on every image: this is the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(1)}"></span> of shape 4 × 32; in part 9 we denoted its elements <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\delta^{(1)}"></span>. Take the column of neuron 22 from it: four numbers, one per image.</p><p>A minus for the three, the five and the eight means the loss will drop if the neuron's sum grows on these images. A plus for the two means it drops if the sum shrinks.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="imgs sig prod" data-focus="prod"><div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · contributions</div><h4>Each image multiplied by its signal</h4><p>The weight <span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(1)}_{k,22}"></span> enters the sum of neuron 22 as the term <span class="math-inline" data-tex="x_k\, w^{(1)}_{k,22}"></span>, so an image's contribution to its derivative is the brightness of cell <span class="math-inline" data-tex="k"></span> times the signal (part 9, step 6). For all 64 cells at once this is the image multiplied by one number.</p><p>The three, the five and the eight turn blue, the two red. Empty cells stay gray: zero times any signal is zero.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="imgs sig prod sum cell" data-focus="sum cell"><div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · the sum</div><h4>The sum of four maps is column 22 of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span></h4><p>The contributions of the batch's images add up, so the four maps are added cell by cell. This gives 64 numbers, column 22 of the matrix <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)} = X^{\top} \partial L/\partial Z^{(1)}"></span>, folded back into 8 × 8. The circled cell is the one we computed in part 10:</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} \frac{\partial L}{\partial w^{(1)}_{2,22}} = 0.0625\cdot(-0.0661) + 0 + 0.1875\cdot 0.0486 + 0 \\ = 0.0050 \end{gathered}"></div></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="imgs sig prod sum upd" data-focus="sum upd"><div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · what the step will do</div><h4>Blue cells will grow, red ones will shrink</h4><p>A descent step subtracts the derivative times <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\eta = 0.3"></span> (part 12). Where the map is blue, the weight of neuron 22 will grow; where it is red, it will shrink; where it is gray, it will not change.</p><p>There are 41 blue cells, and they lie on the strokes of the three, the five and the eight. There are 5 red ones, all where the light two is. After the step neuron 22 responds more to the three, the five and the eight and less to the two, exactly as the signs of the signals in step 1 demanded.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="grid" data-focus="grid"><div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · all neurons</div><h4>32 neurons, 32 maps, 10 of them empty</h4><p>Every column of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> is folded the same way. Ten neurons (1, 2, 4, 6, 10, 20, 21, 27, 30, 31) are closed by ReLU on all four images: their signal is zero everywhere, and the map is empty. The same ten neurons give zero rows in <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(2)}"></span>: their value <span class="math-inline" data-tex="h"></span> is zero, and the weights leaving them had no effect on this batch.</p><p>A neuron open on only one image gets a copy of it multiplied by the signal: for neurons 3, 19, 24 and 28 it is the five, for 25, 26 and 29 the eight.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="grid empty" data-focus="empty"><div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · empty cells</div><h4>18 rows of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> are exactly zero</h4><p>The gray cells along the edges sit in the same places on all 22 maps: these are cells empty in all four images of the batch. An image's contribution is the cell's brightness times the signal, and the brightness is zero, so the row of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> for that cell is zero for any signals. There are 18 such cells: the whole left and right edges and two cells at the top right. The weights of these cells will not move on this batch.</p><p>Four cells are empty in all 1347 training images; on the small map they are darker. Their 128 weights did not change once in 1260 training steps.</p></div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="grid chk" data-focus="chk"><div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · the check</div><h4>A discrepancy of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="3.7 \cdot 10^{-11}"></span> over all 2410 parameters</h4><p>Each parameter in turn is shifted by ±<span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-5}"></span>, the loss is recomputed twice, and the derivative is taken as <span class="math-inline" data-tex="(L_{+} - L_{-})/2\varepsilon"></span>. The worst discrepancy with the backward pass is <span class="math-inline" data-tex="3.7\cdot 10^{-11}"></span>, which is rounding error. The zero rows and columns matched in both versions. So all 32 maps in the diagram are computed correctly.</p></div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> a gradient almost always has telling zeros, and code is
  checked by them: zero rows of <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(1)}"></span> are cells empty across the whole batch, zero rows of
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial W^{(2)}"></span> are neurons the batch did not wake up, zeros in <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\partial L/\partial Z^{(1)}"></span> are neurons closed by ReLU. If there are fewer zeros
  than there should be, a mask got lost somewhere.
</div>

---

## Part 12. The step: where and how far to move 2410 numbers

<p>
  Why the step must go exactly against the gradient follows from expanding the loss at the point where we stand.
  Collect all 2410 numbers into one vector θ, and all derivatives into the vector
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="g = \nabla L"></span>. For a small shift in the direction of
  a unit vector u, the first term of the Taylor expansion looks like this:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="L(\theta + t\,u) \;\approx\; L(\theta) + t\,\langle g,\,u\rangle"></div>

<p>
  The dot product <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\langle g, u\rangle"></span> for
  a unit-length u cannot be less than <span class="math-inline" data-tex="-\|g\|"></span>,
  and equality is reached exactly at <span class="math-inline" data-tex="u = -g/\|g\|"></span>.
  That is, for a small step the direction against the gradient decreases the loss faster than any other. Hence the rule, one for all parameters at once, with no exceptions for weights,
  biases or layers:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="\theta \;\leftarrow\; \theta - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}"></div>

<p>Gradient descent itself, without a network, on the simplest problem is covered in the article <a href="article.html?slug=gradient-descent">“Gradient descent on two points”</a>. It also covers stochastic descent and momentum.</p>

<p>
  Let's see step by step what this rule looks like on the matrices themselves, and what happens to the
  numbers we computed by hand in parts 7 and 10.
</p>

<foreignObject x="40.0" y="358.4" width="770" height="29.9"><div xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml" class="svg-math svg-math-fit" style="font-size:13px;color:#5E5850;font-weight:400"><span><span data-tex="\eta"></span> is the step length (learning rate); all numbers are computed on the same batch of four images</span></div></foreignObject>

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mmall e1" data-focus="e1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · the rule</div>
      <h4>Each number has its derivative subtracted</h4>
<p>The backward pass gave 2410 derivatives. A descent step is one line, the same for weights and biases, for the first layer and the second: subtract the derivative times the step length η.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}, \qquad \eta = 0.3"></div><p>The minus here is essential: the derivative shows where the loss <em>grows</em>, and we need the opposite direction.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm2 e1 h1" data-focus="h1">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · one cell</div>
      <h4><span class="math-inline" data-tex="w^{(2)}_{22,4}"></span>: 0.2681 → 0.3162</h4>
<p>The very weight between neuron 22 and class “3” for which we computed the derivative −0.1604 by hand. It is negative, so subtracting it will increase the weight.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="w^{(2)}_{22,4} \leftarrow 0.2681 - 0.3\cdot(-0.1604) = 0.2681 + 0.0481 = 0.3162"></div><p>The meaning reads literally: the correct class was the three, neuron 22 was active, so the connection between them should be strengthened. The network just did that, knowing nothing about threes or digits.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm3 e2" data-focus="e2">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · biases</div>
      <h4>They were zeros, now they are ten different numbers</h4>
<p>The biases were initialized with zeros, so after the first step they are simply −η times the derivative.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} b^{(2)}_{4} = 0 - 0.3\cdot(-0.1190) = 0.0357 \\ b^{(2)}_{1} = 0 - 0.3\cdot 0.1076 = -0.0323 \end{gathered}"></div><p>Classes the network named wrongly got negative biases; correct classes got positive ones. The sum of all ten derivatives is zero, so the sum of the new biases is zero too: softmax cannot be shifted as a whole, only redistributed.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mm0 mm1 e3 h3" data-focus="h3">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · first layer</div>
      <h4>1134 cells out of 2048 did not change by a single bit</h4>
<p>The formula is exactly the same. The only difference is that the first layer has very many derivatives equal to exactly zero: a pixel empty in all four images or a neuron closed by ReLU.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="w^{(1)}_{2,22} \leftarrow 0.1160 - 0.3\cdot 0.0050 = 0.1146"></div><p>A weight with zero derivative stays the same after the step down to the last bit. The biases <span class="math-inline" data-tex="b^{(1)}"></span> are updated by the same formula; ten of the thirty-two neurons have zero derivative, the same neurons closed on all four images.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mmall e4" data-focus="e4">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · how far the 2410 numbers moved</div>
      <h4>The step length is 6.1% of the length of the weight vector</h4>
<p>All the network's parameters can be treated as one point in a 2410-dimensional space. Then a descent step is a move from point to point, and it has a length.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\|\Delta\theta\| = \eta\,\|\nabla L\| = 0.3\cdot 1.8510 = 0.5553"></div><p>The largest correction to a single number is 0.0633; 1244 parameters get a correction of exactly zero. So the step is not “spread” evenly over the network: it hits the weights that took part in the error on these four images.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mmall e5" data-focus="e5">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · what happened to the loss</div>
      <h4>2.1416 → 1.4731 in one step</h4>
<p>We recompute the forward pass on the same batch with the same formulas, only with the new weights. The probabilities of the correct classes grew for all four images.</p><div class="math-display" data-tex="\begin{gathered} (0.1488;\ 0.1381;\ 0.1099;\ 0.0843) \\ \downarrow \\ (0.1947;\ 0.3284;\ 0.1859;\ 0.2323) \end{gathered}"></div><p>Now all four out of four are guessed; there were two. But it is too early to celebrate: these are exactly the images the gradient was computed on. The network has to be checked on others, which is what the held-out set is for.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="mmall e6" data-focus="e6">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 7 · why we cannot jump straight to the minimum</div>
      <h4>After the step the ReLU mask is already different: 51 open cells instead of 56</h4>
<p>The gradient is a derivative at one specific point, and it is valid only near it. It takes just one step for the network to change qualitatively: some neurons close, some open, and the derivatives are recomputed from scratch.</p><p>So the step is kept small and repeated, 1260 times in our training.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
<p class="stage-hint">Focus the scene and step through it with the ← → keys.</p>

<p>
  We have already taken the step: the loss fell from 2.1416 to 1.4731. The same expansion also gives a promise about the size:
  if we step by η against the gradient, the loss should fall by about
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\eta\,\|g\|^2"></span>. Let's compare with what we got.
  The gradient norm is 1.8510, so
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\|g\|^2 = 3.4260"></span>, and at η = 0.3 the linear forecast
  is:
</p>

<div class="math-display" data-tex="2.1416 - 0.3\cdot 3.4260 \;=\; 1.1138 \qquad \text{versus the actual } 1.4731"></div>

<p>
  The forecast was off by 0.36 on the optimistic side, and it is not rounding. The Taylor expansion
  describes the loss surface as a straight line, but the surface is curved: the further we go, the more
  the actual loss bends upward away from the tangent. This is why η cannot be chosen by a formula,
  and too large a step makes things worse than before: on the same batch η = 3 gives a loss of 2.9051, above the starting one.
  The best step for these four images is 0.95, giving 1.0952, but it should not be taken: it is the minimum
  over four images, not over all 1347, and by adapting to them the network would spoil what it already knew.
</p>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> the backward pass gives the direction and you give the length,
  and the cost of a mistake is asymmetric: too small an η means slow training, too large means
  no training at all.
</div>

---

## Part 13. The loop: batches, epochs, shuffling

<p>
  Everything needed for training is assembled. What remains is to close the loop: take a batch, compute the forward
  pass, the loss, the backward pass, move the parameters, and repeat. The full training loop
  fits in twelve lines:
</p>

<pre><code>for ep in range(1, epochs + 1):
    order = rng.permutation(n)                   # shuffle the images
    for i in range(n // B):
        idx = order[i*B : (i+1)*B if i &lt; n//B - 1 else n]
        Xb, Yb = Xtr[idx], Ytr[idx]
        Z1, H1, Z2, P = forward(Xb)              # forward pass
        dZ2 = (P - Yb) / len(idx)                # backward pass
        dW2, db2 = H1.T @ dZ2, dZ2.sum(0)
        dZ1 = (dZ2 @ W2.T) * (Z1 &gt; 0)
        dW1, db1 = Xb.T @ dZ1, dZ1.sum(0)
        W1 -= eta*dW1; b1 -= eta*db1             # descent step
        W2 -= eta*dW2; b2 -= eta*db2</code></pre>

<p>Let's see step by step what training looks like as a whole.</p>

<div class="stage" id="stageTR" tabindex="0">

<svg id="tr" viewBox="0 0 960 540" role="img" aria-label="The batch strip of one epoch and the loss and accuracy curves over thirty epochs">

  <div class="stage-notes">
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="tape" data-focus="tape">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 1 · what training consists of</div>
      <h4>Step, batch, epoch: three different words</h4>
<p>A step is one cycle of “forward pass → loss → backward pass → update” on one batch. 1347 images with a batch of 32 give 42 steps; the last batch takes the remainder and has 35 images. One pass over all images exactly once is called an epoch.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="tape shuf" data-focus="shuf">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 2 · shuffling</div>
      <h4>Each epoch the batches are made up anew</h4>
<p>If the order is not changed, every epoch the network gets the same 42 gradients in the same order and starts adapting to the order. Shuffling costs one line of code and noticeably affects the result: on data sorted by class, without it accuracy drops from 97.11% to 80.67%.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="tape lossax ltr" data-focus="ltr">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 3 · loss by epoch</div>
      <h4>0.5712 after the first epoch, 0.0266 after the thirtieth</h4>
<p>The first epoch is 42 steps, and they take the loss from 2.3 to 0.57. After that the decline slows down: the easily fixed errors run out, and the hard ones remain. The curve is not perfectly smooth: each point is measured after a random set of batches.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="tape lossax ltr lte gap" data-focus="lte">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 4 · the second curve</div>
      <h4>On the held-out set the loss is higher, and that is normal</h4>
<p>The red curve runs above the blue one all the time: on images the network has not seen, it makes slightly more errors. As long as both fall together, training is going right. The moment the blue one keeps falling while the red one turns upward is overfitting.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="tape accax atr ate first" data-focus="first">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 5 · accuracy</div>
      <h4>88.44% already after the first epoch</h4>
<p>Forty-two steps of 32 images, and the network recognizes nine digits out of ten; after the fifth epoch, 95.56%. This is what a typical learning curve looks like: most of the quality is gained at the very beginning, and the last percents cost dozens of epochs.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="step-panel" data-on="tape accax atr ate" data-focus="ate">
      <div class="step-kicker">Step 6 · how it all ended</div>
      <h4>97.78% on the held-out set, 99.78% on the training set</h4>
<p>By the thirtieth epoch the network gets 10 images out of 450 wrong. On the training set there are three errors: it has almost learned it by heart. The gap between the two numbers is the price paid for the finite size of the data.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<p>The whole loop from this part fits in the browser: the same network, the same images, the same batch order as in the NumPy run.</p>

<div class="hn-live" id="wiTrain"></div>

<div class="callout">
  <strong>Key idea of this part:</strong> training is the same cycle of five actions, repeated
  1260 times. Nothing happens at any step except what we have already taken apart; the whole difference between
  an untrained and a trained network accumulates through small shifts of 2410 numbers.
</div>

---

## Part 14. What to be able to reconstruct from memory

<ol class="end-list">
  <li><strong>Data is two matrices.</strong> X of shape B × 64 and Y of shape B × 10 with the same number
  of rows. An image becomes a row, a label becomes a row with a single one and nine zeros.</li>
  <li><strong>The network is 2410 numbers plus a rule for applying them.</strong> Weights and biases live between
  batches; activations are born and die within one step.</li>
  <li><strong>The forward pass is two matrix multiplications and two element-wise operations.</strong>
  Z = XW + b changes the shape and mixes numbers; ReLU and softmax keep the shape.</li>
  <li><strong>The loss is one number, and it has a reference point.</strong> For ten classes an untrained
  network gives ln 10 = 2.3026; our batch gave 2.1416.</li>
  <li><strong>The backward pass starts with (P − Y)/B.</strong> Softmax and cross-entropy together give
  the difference “output minus needed”, and this difference sums to zero along a row.</li>
  <li><strong>A weight's gradient is the layer's input, transposed and multiplied by the output gradient.</strong>
  The shape of a gradient always matches the shape of what we differentiate with respect to; backward, ReLU works as a mask.</li>
  <li><strong>The backward pass must be checked with central differences.</strong> A discrepancy of the order of
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-10}"></span> means “correct”; anything noticeably larger is a bug in the code, not in ε.</li>
  <li><strong>The step: <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \partial L/\partial \theta"></span>, the same for all parameters.</strong> The gradient gives the direction,
  you choose the length, and the right length depends on the scale of the inputs: without dividing by 16 the same η breaks training.</li>
  <li><strong>An epoch = all images once, a step = one batch.</strong> Before each epoch the data
  is shuffled; 1347 images with a batch of 32 give 42 steps.</li>
</ol>

<p>
  If you take one picture away from the article, let it be this: training is a cycle
  of five actions, and we computed each of them by hand. A batch of numbers goes forward, turns
  into one number, this number travels back and leaves a derivative on every parameter, the parameters
  move by a fraction of a percent, and so on 1260 times. Everything called “the network learned to recognize
  digits” is the accumulated result of 1260 small, fully understandable shifts.
</p>

<p class="tiny">
  All numbers in the article are computed on the digits dataset from scikit-learn (1797 images of 8 × 8, values 0…16)
  with our own NumPy implementation of the network: a 1347/450 split stratified by class, a
  64 → 32 → 10 network with ReLU and softmax, weights initialized from a normal distribution with scale
  <span class="math-inline" data-tex="\sqrt{2/n_{\text{in}}}"></span> and a fixed seed,
  batch 32, learning rate 0.3, 30 epochs. The running example is the first four images of the first batch
  of the first epoch. The analytic gradients are checked against central differences with ε = <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-5}"></span> for all
  2410 parameters; the worst discrepancy is 3.7 · <span class="math-inline" data-tex="10^{-11}"></span>. Rounding is to four decimal places everywhere,
  percentages to two.
</p>

<p class="tiny"><a href="assets/code/mnist8-code.zip" download>Download all the code (mnist8-code.zip)</a>: five files in plain NumPy: data and network, the main run, the running example with a gradient check, the error analysis and six experiments with training settings. It reproduces every number in the article.</p>

  /* Сеть 64 → H → 10, веса построчно: W1[k*H + j], W2[j*10 + c] — как массивы NumPy в C-порядке */
  function Net(H, W1, b1, W2, b2) {

  Net.prototype.grads = function (xs, ys) {

    var dz2 = new Float64Array(10), dz1 = new Float64Array(H), i, j, k, c;

  function mulberry(seed) {

  var DATA = null;
  function load(D) {
    var tr = bytes(D.tr), te = bytes(D.te), d = {RTR: [], RTE: [], XTR: [], XTE: [], XTR1: [], XTE1: [], YTR: [], YTE: []}, i;
    function rows(src, n, R, X, X1) {

    rows(te, 450, d.RTE, d.XTE, d.XTE1);

  IDS.forEach(function (id) { var n = $(id); if (n) el('p', 'hn-status', n, 'Loading the images and network weights…'); });
  fetch(DATA_URL).then(function (r) { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); return r.json(); }).then(function (D) {
    DATA = load(D);

    if (window.console) console.error('how-network-learns data', e);

  });

  /* ======== В1. Клетка → позиция в строке ======== */
  function wCells() {
    var w = setup('wiCells', 'Find a cell in the row', 'Hover over a cell of the image or a position in the row below: the pair lights up. The "shuffle" button lays the cells out in a different, but also fixed, order.');
    if (!w) return;
    var raw = DATA.BR[0], cur = 3, shuffled = false, inv = new Array(64);
    DATA.PIX.forEach(function (cell, pos) { inv[cell] = pos; });
    var ctr = el('div', 'hn-ctrls', w);
    var picks = [0, 1, 2, 3].map(function (i) { return {v: i, t: 'digit ' + DATA.BY[i]}; });
    picks.push({v: -1, t: 'random'});
    chips(ctr, 'image:', picks, 0, function (v) {
      raw = v >= 0 ? DATA.BR[v] : DATA.RTR[Math.floor(Math.random() * 1347)]; draw();
    });
    toggle(ctr, 'shuffle the cell order', false, function (on) { shuffled = on; draw(); });
    var row = el('div', 'hn-row', w);
    var left = el('div', 'hn-fix', row), gb = svgBox(left, 288, 288);
    var side = el('div', 'hn-side', row), read = el('div', 'hn-read', side);
    var fold = el('div', 'hn-fix', side); fold.style.marginTop = '8px';
    var sb = svgBox(w, 680, 86);
    sb.panel.style.marginTop = '12px';
    function posOf(k) { return shuffled ? inv[k] : k; }
    function cellAt(pos) { return shuffled ? DATA.PIX[pos] : pos; }
    function draw() {
      clear(gb.svg); clear(sb.svg);
      for (var k = 0; k < 64; k++) {
        var x = (k % 8) * 36, y = Math.floor(k / 8) * 36, v = raw[k];
        var r = S('rect', {x: x, y: y, width: 36, height: 36, fill: grayOf(v), stroke: C.line, 'stroke-width': 0.8}, gb.svg);
        T(gb.svg, x + 18, y + 23, String(v), {'text-anchor': 'middle', 'font-size': 13, fill: v >= 9 ? '#FFFFFF' : C.gray, 'pointer-events': 'none'});
        hook(r, k);
      }
      for (var pos = 0; pos < 64; pos++) {
        var kk = cellAt(pos);
        var rr = S('rect', {x: 20 + pos * 10, y: 8, width: 10, height: 34, fill: grayOf(raw[kk]), stroke: C.line, 'stroke-width': 0.4}, sb.svg);
        hook(rr, kk);
        if (pos % 8 === 0) T(sb.svg, 20 + pos * 10 + 1, 60, String(pos + 1), {'font-size': 11});
      }
      S('rect', {x: 20, y: 8, width: 640, height: 34, fill: 'none', stroke: C.blue, 'stroke-width': 1.4}, sb.svg);
      T(sb.svg, 660, 80, 'position number in the row x', {'font-size': 11, 'text-anchor': 'end'});
      gb.hl = S('rect', {width: 36, height: 36, fill: 'none', stroke: C.red, 'stroke-width': 3, 'pointer-events': 'none'}, gb.svg);
      sb.hl = S('rect', {y: 3, width: 10, height: 44, fill: 'none', stroke: C.red, 'stroke-width': 2.4, 'pointer-events': 'none'}, sb.svg);
      clear(fold);
      if (shuffled) {
        var fb = svgBox(fold, 260, 120);
        var perm = new Uint8Array(64);
        for (var q = 0; q < 64; q++) perm[q] = raw[DATA.PIX[q]];
        thumb(fb.svg, perm, 10, 10, 12.5);
        T(fb.svg, 120, 40, 'the row,', {'font-size': 12});
        T(fb.svg, 120, 56, 'folded', {'font-size': 12});
        T(fb.svg, 120, 72, 'back', {'font-size': 12});
        T(fb.svg, 120, 88, 'into 8 × 8', {'font-size': 12});
      }
      select(cur);
    }
    function hook(node, k) {
      node.style.cursor = 'pointer';
      node.addEventListener('pointerenter', function () { select(k); });
      node.addEventListener('click', function () { select(k); });
    }
    function select(k) {
      cur = k;
      var r = Math.floor(k / 8) + 1, c = k % 8 + 1, pos = posOf(k) + 1, v = raw[k];
      gb.hl.setAttribute('x', (k % 8) * 36); gb.hl.setAttribute('y', Math.floor(k / 8) * 36);
      sb.hl.setAttribute('x', 20 + (pos - 1) * 10);
      clear(read);
      p(read, 'cell: row ' + r + ', column ' + c, 'hn-big');
      if (shuffled) p(read, 'position in the row: ' + pos + ', set by the permutation table, not by a formula');
      else p(read, 'position: $k = 8(r-1) + c = 8\\cdot' + (r - 1) + ' + ' + c + ' = ' + pos + '$');
